terms.label: absolute immunity
terms.gloss: Complete protection from a lawsuit, or claimed protection from being forced to testify, covering acts within a protected role however wrongful, unlike qualified immunity, which can be overcome.

terms.label: absolute privilege
terms.gloss: A complete defense to defamation for statements made in certain settings, such as court proceedings or legislative debate, even if false or made with ill will.

terms.label: abstention
terms.gloss: A federal court's decision to decline or postpone deciding a case it has power to hear, out of respect for state courts or related state proceedings.

terms.label: abstract of title
terms.gloss: A summary of the public records affecting a piece of land, such as sales, mortgages, and liens, used to trace and show who owns it.

terms.label: abuse of discretion
terms.gloss: A deferential standard of review: an appeals court overturns a trial judge's judgment call only if it was clearly unreasonable, legally mistaken, or unsupported.

terms.label: abuse of process
terms.gloss: The civil wrong of misusing a court procedure, such as a subpoena, attachment, or arrest, for an improper purpose it was not designed to serve.

terms.label: acceleration (of a debt)
terms.gloss: A creditor's right, usually under a contract term, to demand the entire remaining debt at once after a default, instead of in later installments.

terms.label: accessory before the fact
terms.gloss: A person who helps plan or encourages a crime but is not present when it is committed.

terms.label: accommodation shipment (UCC)
terms.gloss: Goods a seller ships while telling the buyer they do not match the order, offered only as a favor. Under UCC § 2-206 that shipment is a new offer, not an acceptance.

terms.label: accord and satisfaction
terms.gloss: An agreement to accept a different performance, often a smaller payment, to settle a disputed debt (the accord), plus that performance (the satisfaction), which ends the original claim.

terms.label: account stated
terms.gloss: A claim that a debtor agreed, expressly or by not objecting in time, that a statement of the balance owed was correct, so the creditor can sue on that balance.

terms.label: accounting (court remedy)
terms.gloss: A court-ordered remedy requiring someone who handled another's money or property, such as a partner, agent, or trustee, to disclose the full figures and pay over what is owed.

terms.label: accrue
terms.gloss: For a legal claim, to come into existence, usually when the injury happens; the deadline for filing suit generally starts running then.

terms.label: act of state doctrine
terms.gloss: A doctrine under which U.S. courts generally refuse to judge the lawfulness of a foreign government's official acts done within its own territory.

terms.label: action (lawsuit)
terms.gloss: A lawsuit: a case one party brings against another in court. Here it does not mean an act or deed.

terms.label: action on the case
terms.gloss: An old common-law lawsuit for indirect or consequential harm, as opposed to trespass, which covered direct, forcible injury. Modern negligence claims grew from it.

terms.label: actionable
terms.gloss: Giving grounds for a lawsuit: conduct the law lets someone sue over, if it is proven. Not the business sense of 'practical' or 'ready to act on'.

terms.label: actual malice
terms.gloss: In defamation since New York Times v. Sullivan (1964), knowing a statement was false or recklessly disregarding whether it was. In older cases and privilege rules, spite or an improper motive.

terms.label: ad valorem
terms.gloss: Latin for 'according to value': a tax or duty set as a percentage of an item's value rather than a fixed amount.

terms.label: adequacy of representation
terms.gloss: The requirement that those speaking for a group in a lawsuit will fairly protect its interests. In class actions it tests the named representatives and their lawyers for conflicts and competence.

terms.label: adequate assurance of performance
terms.gloss: When one party reasonably doubts the other will perform, it may demand written assurance and suspend its own performance until it gets it. Failing to give assurance can count as repudiation.

terms.label: adequate remedy at law
terms.gloss: Money damages or another ordinary remedy that would fully fix the harm. Courts of equity traditionally grant injunctions only when none exists.

terms.label: adhesion contract
terms.gloss: A standard-form contract drafted by the stronger party and offered on a take-it-or-leave-it basis, with no chance to bargain over terms.

terms.label: adjudication (by an agency)

terms.gloss: An agency deciding a specific case about particular parties, much as a court does, rather than making general rules for the future. Formal adjudication uses trial-type hearings.

terms.label: adjudicative facts
terms.gloss: Facts about the particular parties and events in a dispute (who did what, where, and when), as opposed to general facts that inform a policy or rule.

terms.label: adjustment of status
terms.gloss: The process by which a noncitizen already in the United States becomes a lawful permanent resident (gets a green card) without leaving the country.

terms.label: administrative law judge (ALJ)
terms.gloss: A hearing officer within a government agency who holds trial-like hearings and issues decisions, which the agency's leaders can usually review and change.

terms.label: administrator ad prosequendum
terms.gloss: A person a court appoints only to bring a lawsuit for a dead person's estate or survivors, such as a wrongful-death claim, not to manage the whole estate.

terms.label: administratrix / executrix
terms.gloss: Older terms for a woman who manages a dead person's estate: an executrix is named in the will; an administratrix is chosen by a court, usually when there is no will.

terms.label: admiralty
terms.gloss: Maritime law, covering ships, shipping, and sea commerce. Federal courts hear these cases under special rules, traditionally without a jury.

terms.label: adverse possession
terms.gloss: A way to gain ownership of land by openly, continuously, and exclusively occupying it without the owner's permission for a period set by law, often 10 to 20 years.

terms.label: advisory opinion
terms.gloss: A court's answer to a legal question when there is no real dispute before it. Federal courts may not give them under Article III, though some state courts may.

terms.label: advisory verdict
terms.gloss: A jury's finding that the judge may consider but need not follow, because the judge, not the jury, decides the issue.

terms.label: affiant
terms.gloss: The person who makes and signs a sworn written statement (an affidavit).

terms.label: affidavit
terms.gloss: A written statement of facts that the writer swears or affirms is true, signed before an official such as a notary, and usable as evidence.

terms.label: affirmative defense
terms.gloss: A defendant's own reason for defeating a claim even if the plaintiff's allegations are true, such as a privilege or the statute of limitations. The defendant must raise and usually prove it.

terms.label: agency (principal and agent)
terms.gloss: A relationship in which one person, the agent, acts on behalf of and under the control of another, the principal. Not a government agency.

terms.label: alias process (summons)
terms.gloss: A second summons or other court paper issued after the first was not successfully served. Here 'alias' does not mean a false name.

terms.label: allotment (Indian land)
terms.gloss: Under federal Indian policy from about 1887 to 1934, a parcel of reservation land assigned to an individual tribal member; leftover 'surplus' land was often opened to non-Indian settlers.

terms.label: alter ego
terms.gloss: A company or person so controlled by another that a court treats the two as one, disregarding the separate corporate form, often to make the owner pay the company's debts.

terms.label: amicus curiae (plural: amici)
terms.gloss: Latin for 'friend of the court': a nonparty allowed to file arguments because it has an interest in the case or useful expertise.

terms.label: amount in controversy
terms.gloss: The money at stake in a lawsuit, as claimed by the plaintiff. For a federal diversity case it must today exceed $75,000, not counting interest and costs.

terms.label: answer (pleading)
terms.gloss: The defendant's formal written response to a complaint, admitting or denying each allegation and raising any defenses.

terms.label: antenuptial (prenuptial) agreement
terms.gloss: A contract made before marriage setting each spouse's property rights, and sometimes support, if the marriage ends by divorce or death. Also called a prenuptial agreement.

terms.label: apparent authority
terms.gloss: An agent's power to bind the person or company it acts for, because that party led an outsider to reasonably believe the agent had permission, even though it did not.

terms.label: appearance (special or general)
terms.gloss: Formally taking part in a case before a court. A special appearance contests the court's power over the defendant without accepting it; a general appearance accepts that power.

terms.label: appellee
terms.gloss: The party responding to an appeal, usually the side that won in the lower court. The party bringing the appeal is the appellant.

terms.label: Appointments Clause
terms.gloss: The constitutional provision on filling federal offices: the President appoints principal officers with Senate consent, and Congress may let the President, courts, or department heads appoint lesser officers.

terms.label: arbitrability
terms.gloss: Whether a particular dispute falls within an agreement to arbitrate, and so must go to an arbitrator instead of a court.

terms.label: arbitrary and capricious (review)
terms.gloss: The usual test courts apply to agency decisions: the agency must have considered the relevant factors and explained a rational link between the facts and its choice.

terms.label: arising under (federal-question jurisdiction)
terms.context: \b(aris(ing|es|e)|arose) under (federal law|the Constitution|the laws of the United States|federal|a federal|treat(y|ies))|well-pleaded|\b1331\b
terms.gloss: Describes a case whose claim is created by federal law or necessarily depends on a substantial federal question. Federal courts may hear such cases.

terms.label: Article I court (legislative court)
terms.gloss: A tribunal Congress creates outside the regular federal judiciary, such as the Tax Court, whose judges lack life tenure. The cases it may decide are limited.

terms.label: Article III
terms.gloss: The part of the U.S. Constitution that creates the federal courts and limits them to real 'cases' and 'controversies', so a plaintiff there must show an actual injury.

terms.label: as-applied challenge
terms.gloss: A claim that a law is unconstitutional only as used against this particular person or conduct, leaving it enforceable in other situations.

terms.label: assignment (of rights)
terms.gloss: A transfer of a contract right or other legal claim from its holder (the assignor) to someone else (the assignee), who can then enforce it.

terms.label: assizes
terms.gloss: Periodic court sessions held in English counties by judges traveling from London on circuit, to try civil and criminal cases before local juries.

terms.label: associational standing
terms.gloss: An organization's right to sue on behalf of its members when they could sue themselves, the case relates to the group's purpose, and individual members need not take part.

terms.label: assumpsit
terms.gloss: An old common-law lawsuit for breaking a promise or for money owed. It developed into the modern claims for breach of contract and for restitution.

terms.label: assumption of risk
terms.gloss: A defense that the injured person knowingly and voluntarily accepted a known danger, which can reduce or bar their recovery.

terms.label: at law (vs. in equity)
terms.gloss: Belonging to the historic courts of law, which mainly awarded money damages and used juries, as opposed to courts of equity, which issued orders like injunctions without juries.

terms.label: at will
terms.gloss: Able to be ended by either side at any time, for a good reason, a bad reason, or none, though not for an illegal reason such as discrimination. Most U.S. jobs are at will by default.

terms.label: attachment (of property)
terms.gloss: A court order seizing or freezing a defendant's property, often before trial, so it can later pay a judgment or give the court power over the case.

terms.label: attaint (writ)
terms.gloss: An old English writ for challenging a jury's false verdict before a larger jury of twenty-four. If it succeeded, the verdict was reversed and the original jurors were punished.

terms.label: attorney-in-fact
terms.gloss: Someone authorized in writing to act for another person, usually under a power of attorney. Not necessarily a lawyer.

terms.label: Auer deference
terms.gloss: Courts' practice of accepting an agency's reasonable reading of its own ambiguous regulation. Kisor v. Wilkie (2019) kept it but limited it to genuinely ambiguous rules.

terms.label: automatic stay
terms.gloss: The freeze on most collection efforts and lawsuits against a debtor that takes effect automatically, without a court order, as soon as a bankruptcy case is filed.

terms.label: bailment
terms.gloss: Handing personal property to someone to hold for a purpose, such as storage or shipping, without giving up ownership. The holder is the bailee; the owner is the bailor.

terms.label: preference (bankruptcy)
terms.gloss: A payment a debtor made to a creditor shortly before bankruptcy, usually within 90 days, that the bankruptcy trustee can take back to share fairly among all creditors.

terms.label: basic assumption
terms.gloss: A fact or condition both parties took for granted when contracting. If it was mistaken, or an unexpected event destroys it, mistake, impracticability, or frustration may excuse performance.

terms.label: bench trial
terms.gloss: A trial decided by a judge alone, with no jury, so the judge finds the facts as well as applying the law.

terms.label: beneficial interest
terms.gloss: The right to enjoy property's benefits, such as its use or income, even though someone else, like a trustee or nominal holder, holds the legal title.

terms.label: bill (in equity)
terms.gloss: The old name for the plaintiff's opening pleading in a court of equity, roughly what is now called a complaint.

terms.label: bill of exceptions
terms.gloss: Exceptions are formal objections to a trial judge's rulings, or to a court-appointed official's report; a bill of exceptions sets them out in writing so a higher court can review them.

terms.label: bill of exchange
terms.gloss: A signed written order directing someone to pay a fixed sum of money to another, on demand or on a set date. A check is a modern example.

terms.label: bill of lading
terms.gloss: A document a carrier gives a shipper listing goods accepted for transport; it serves as a receipt and can control who may claim the goods.

terms.label: bill of particulars
terms.gloss: A more detailed written statement of the charges or claims, which a court can order so the other side knows exactly what it must answer or defend against.

terms.label: binder (insurance)
terms.gloss: A short, temporary insurance contract giving coverage right away until the full policy is issued.

terms.label: brief (written argument)
terms.gloss: A party's written argument to a court, setting out the facts and legal reasons for the ruling it wants. 'Briefing' is the exchange of these papers.

terms.label: bucket shop
terms.gloss: An illegal business, common around 1900, that took bets on stock or commodity price changes without actually buying or selling anything.

terms.label: burden of persuasion
terms.gloss: A party's duty to convince the factfinder that its version is true to the required degree, such as more likely than not. If the evidence is evenly balanced, that party loses.

terms.label: burden of production
terms.gloss: A party's duty to offer enough evidence on a point for the factfinder to consider it; otherwise the judge can decide the point against them. It can shift between sides.

terms.label: business-records exception
terms.gloss: A rule letting records kept in the regular course of business be used as evidence, despite the usual bar on out-of-court statements, if a qualified witness or certification shows how they were kept.

terms.label: but-for cause
terms.gloss: A cause without which the result would not have happened: if the act had not occurred, the harm would not have occurred either.

terms.label: by operation of law
terms.gloss: Automatically, because a legal rule says so, without anyone agreeing to it or taking any action.

terms.label: cancellation of removal
terms.gloss: Immigration relief letting certain noncitizens in deportation proceedings stay and become lawful permanent residents if they meet strict requirements.

terms.label: canon of construction
terms.gloss: A standard rule of thumb judges use to interpret legal texts, such as giving every word effect or reading unclear contract terms against the drafter.

terms.label: capable of repetition, yet evading review
match: capable of repetition, yet evading review
capable of repetition yet evading review
terms.gloss: An exception to mootness (a dispute that has ended, so a ruling would change nothing): courts may still decide disputes too brief to finish in court that are likely to recur for the same party.

terms.label: capacity (legal)
terms.gloss: The legal ability to do a binding legal act, such as make a contract or will, or bring a suit. Minors and people with serious mental impairments may lack it.

terms.label: case or controversy
terms.gloss: Article III's limit that federal courts decide only real, live disputes between parties with a genuine stake in the outcome, not hypothetical questions or requests for advice.

terms.label: cassation
terms.gloss: Review by France's highest court for civil and criminal cases, or a similar civil-law court, limited to errors of law. It can annul a lower judgment and send the case to another court.

terms.label: cause of action
terms.gloss: A recognized legal basis for suing: a set of facts that, if proven, entitles the plaintiff to a court-ordered remedy. One complaint can plead several.

terms.label: certified question
terms.gloss: A legal question one court formally sends to another, usually a state's highest court, to answer before the sending court decides the case, typically because no clear precedent exists.

terms.label: certiorari
terms.gloss: A higher court's order agreeing to review a lower court's decision. The U.S. Supreme Court grants it to choose the small share of cases it will hear.

terms.label: challenge for cause
terms.gloss: A request to remove a potential juror for a specific reason, such as bias or a tie to a party. Unlike peremptory challenges, which need no reason, they are unlimited in number.

terms.label: challenge to the array
terms.gloss: An objection to the whole pool of potential jurors, claiming it was assembled improperly, rather than an objection to any single juror.

terms.label: chancellor (equity judge)
terms.gloss: The judge of a court of equity (chancery), which grants remedies like injunctions rather than money damages. Some states, such as Delaware, still use the title.

terms.label: chancery
terms.gloss: A court of equity, which historically gave remedies such as injunctions that ordinary law courts could not. England's Court of Chancery was the model; Delaware still has one.

terms.label: chattel
terms.gloss: Movable personal property, such as goods or animals, as opposed to land and buildings.

terms.label: Chenery doctrine
terms.gloss: The rule that a court judges an agency action only by the reasons the agency gave when it acted, not by new reasons its lawyers offer later.

terms.label: Chevron deference
terms.gloss: The former rule that courts accept an agency's reasonable reading of an unclear statute it administers. The Supreme Court overruled it in Loper Bright (2024).

terms.label: choice of law
terms.gloss: The rules a court uses to decide which state's or country's law governs a dispute. A choice-of-law clause is the contracting parties' own pick.

terms.label: c.i.f. (cost, insurance, and freight)
terms.gloss: A shipping term: the price covers the goods plus insurance and freight to a named destination port. The seller performs by shipping the goods and handing over the shipping documents.

terms.label: claim preclusion (res judicata)
terms.gloss: The rule that a final judgment on the merits bars the same parties from suing again on the same claim, including grounds they could have raised the first time.

terms.label: class certification
terms.gloss: A court's order letting a lawsuit proceed as a class action, after finding the proposed class and its representatives meet Rule 23's requirements. Decertification undoes that order.

terms.label: clear and convincing evidence
terms.gloss: A middle standard of proof: the claim must be shown to be highly probable, more than 'more likely than not' but less than beyond a reasonable doubt.

terms.label: clear-statement rule
terms.gloss: A rule that courts will not read a statute to produce a major result, such as overriding states' traditional powers or waiving immunity, unless Congress said so in unmistakable terms.

terms.label: clearly erroneous (clear error)
terms.gloss: A deferential standard for reviewing a trial judge's findings of fact: the appeals court keeps them unless it is firmly convinced a mistake was made.

terms.label: codicil
terms.gloss: A later written amendment to a will that adds to or changes it without replacing it.

terms.label: cognizable
terms.gloss: Recognized by law as a kind of claim or harm that a court can hear and remedy.

terms.label: cognizance
terms.gloss: An older word for a court's authority to hear and decide a particular kind of case, close to what is now called subject-matter jurisdiction.

terms.label: collateral attack
terms.gloss: A challenge to a judgment made in a separate, later case rather than by appeal. It usually succeeds only for basic defects, such as the first court's lack of jurisdiction.

terms.label: collateral order doctrine
terms.gloss: A narrow exception to waiting for the end of a case to appeal: an important, conclusive ruling, separate from the main dispute, that could not be fixed later can be appealed at once.

terms.label: collective action (FLSA)
terms.gloss: A group lawsuit by workers for unpaid wages under the Fair Labor Standards Act. Unlike a class action, each worker must opt in by filing written consent.

terms.label: color of law
terms.gloss: Acting with the apparent authority of government, as an official does, even when misusing or exceeding that authority. Federal civil-rights suits under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 require action under color of state law.

terms.label: colorable
terms.gloss: Plausible or arguable on its face: strong enough to deserve serious consideration, even if it may not ultimately prove correct.

terms.label: comity
terms.gloss: The respect one court or government gives to another's laws and decisions out of courtesy rather than legal obligation, such as federal restraint toward state courts.

terms.label: committed to agency discretion
match: committed to agency discretion by law
terms.gloss: A narrow exception to court review: some agency choices, such as whether to bring an enforcement action, are left to the agency because no legal standard exists to judge them by.

terms.label: common carrier
terms.gloss: A business that offers to carry goods, passengers, or messages for the general public, and so must serve all comers on reasonable, nondiscriminatory terms.

terms.label: common law
terms.gloss: Law developed by judges through decisions in individual cases, rather than law enacted by a legislature.

terms.label: common nucleus of operative fact
terms.gloss: A shared core of facts underlying two claims. When a state claim and a federal claim share one, a federal court may hear both together.

terms.label: commonality (Rule 23(a)(2))
terms.gloss: The class-action requirement that members share a common question whose answer will resolve an issue central to every member's claim in one stroke.

terms.label: community property
terms.gloss: In some states, such as California and Arizona, property acquired during a marriage (other than by gift or inheritance), which belongs equally to both spouses no matter who earned it.

terms.label: compensatory damages
terms.gloss: Money meant to make up for the actual loss or harm the plaintiff suffered, as opposed to money meant to punish the wrongdoer.

terms.label: competent evidence
terms.gloss: Evidence the law allows a court to consider because it is relevant and admissible. 'Competent' here does not mean skilled or convincing.

terms.label: complaint
terms.gloss: The document a plaintiff files to start a lawsuit, setting out the facts, the legal claims, and what the plaintiff asks the court to order.

terms.label: compromise
terms.gloss: To settle a disputed claim by agreement, each side giving up part of what it wanted, so the dispute ends without a court deciding who was right.

terms.label: compulsory counterclaim
terms.gloss: A defendant's claim against the plaintiff arising from the same transaction or events. It must be raised in the same lawsuit or it is usually lost.

terms.label: compulsory joinder
terms.gloss: The rule (Federal Rule 19) requiring certain absent persons to be added to a lawsuit when it cannot fairly go on without them; if they cannot be added, it may be dismissed.

terms.label: concerted activity
terms.gloss: Employees acting together for mutual aid or protection, such as organizing a union or jointly raising workplace complaints. The National Labor Relations Act protects it from employer interference.

terms.label: conclusory
terms.gloss: Stating a conclusion, such as 'the defendant acted unlawfully,' without the specific facts that would support it. Courts give such statements little or no weight.

terms.label: concurrence (concurring opinion)
terms.gloss: A separate opinion by a judge who agrees with the result but adds or substitutes reasons. To concur is to agree with the result.

terms.label: concurrence in the judgment
match: concurred in part and in the judgment
concurred in the judgment in part
terms.gloss: A judge's vote agreeing with the outcome but not with the majority's reasoning, usually explained in a separate opinion. The judge does not join the majority's explanation.

terms.label: condemnation (taking of property)
terms.gloss: Not criticism: the government's forced taking of private property for a public use, such as a road, which the Constitution requires it to pay for fairly.

terms.label: condemnation (forfeiture)
terms.gloss: In admiralty and customs cases, a court's judgment declaring seized property, such as a ship or cargo, forfeited to the government or its captors. Not a taking for public use.

terms.label: condition precedent
terms.gloss: An event that must happen before a party's duty to perform under a contract arises. If it never occurs, the duty never becomes due.

terms.label: conditional legislation
terms.gloss: A law that takes effect, or changes, only when an official finds that a stated condition exists. It was an early way courts approved giving power to the executive.

terms.label: conditional privilege
terms.gloss: In defamation, a defense protecting statements made for a legitimate purpose, such as an employer explaining a firing. Unlike absolute privilege, it is lost if abused or made with malice.

terms.label: conference report
terms.gloss: A report from the joint House-Senate committee that settles differences between the two chambers' versions of a bill. Courts often treat it as especially reliable evidence of what Congress meant.

terms.label: confirm (an arbitration award)
terms.gloss: To turn an arbitrator's award into an enforceable court judgment, or to ask a court to do so.

terms.label: consent decree
terms.gloss: An order of a court or agency whose terms the parties agreed to, usually to settle a case. Unlike a private settlement, it can be enforced directly as an order.

terms.label: consequential damages
terms.gloss: Compensation for indirect losses that flow from a breach, such as profits lost while a machine sat unrepaired. Recoverable only if foreseeable when the contract was made.

terms.label: conservatorship
terms.gloss: Putting a conservator, appointed by a court or a regulator, in charge of a person's or company's property and affairs to protect and manage them, as with a failing financial firm.

terms.label: consideration (contract)
terms.gloss: What each side gives or promises in exchange for the other's promise. Without such a bargained-for exchange, a promise usually is not an enforceable contract.

terms.label: constitutional avoidance
terms.gloss: The principle that when a statute can reasonably be read two ways, courts choose the reading that avoids serious doubts about its constitutionality.

terms.label: construction (interpretation)
terms.gloss: Interpretation: deciding what a statute, contract, or other legal text means and how it applies. Not building.

terms.label: constructive discharge
terms.gloss: Treating an employee's resignation as a firing because the employer made working conditions so intolerable that a reasonable person would have felt forced to quit.

terms.label: constructive fraud
terms.gloss: Conduct the law treats as fraud even without intent to deceive, such as abusing a position of trust, or a debtor's transfer of property for too little value that harms creditors.

terms.label: constructive notice
terms.gloss: Knowledge the law treats a person as having because a reasonably careful person would have learned it, for example from a public record or posted terms, whether or not they did.

terms.label: constructive trust
terms.gloss: A court-ordered remedy, not a real trust: someone who wrongfully or unjustly obtained property must hold it for, and turn it over to, the person who should have it.

terms.label: continuance
terms.gloss: A court's postponement of a hearing, trial, or deadline to a later date.

terms.label: contra proferentem
terms.gloss: A rule for reading contracts: an unclear term is interpreted against the party that drafted it.

terms.label: contribution (among wrongdoers)
terms.context: \bcontribution,? (or|and) indemn|indemn\w*,? (or|and) contribution|right (to|of) contribution|contribution claims?|bar on contribution|whether contribution|for contribution
terms.gloss: A defendant's right to make others responsible for the same harm pay their fair share of what it has paid, or must pay, the injured person. Not a donation.

terms.label: contributory negligence
terms.gloss: The plaintiff's own carelessness helping cause the injury. In a few places it still bars recovery entirely; most states now just reduce the award (comparative negligence).

terms.label: conversion (tort)
terms.context: \b(fraud\w*|negligen\w*|contract|unjust enrichment|fiduciary|trespass|malpractice|tortious|infringement|replevin|unfair competition|misconduct|possessory|counterclaimed|breach|conversion (claims?|judgment|award|instruction|cases)|(malicious|fraudulent|willful) conversion|constituted conversion|defeated conversion|massachusetts conversion|conversion of (the|a) (horse|mature crop))\b
terms.gloss: Not a change of form: the civil wrong of seriously interfering with another person's movable property, such as taking, keeping, or destroying it as if it were your own. The owner can recover its value.

terms.label: corporate waste
terms.gloss: Directors' giving away company assets, or spending them for no real benefit, on terms no reasonable businessperson would accept. Shareholders may sue over it on the company's behalf.

terms.label: corpus (of a trust)
terms.gloss: The money or property held in a trust, which the trustee manages for the beneficiaries.

terms.label: count (in a complaint or indictment)
terms.gloss: One separately stated claim in a complaint, or one separately charged crime in an indictment. Each count can succeed or fail on its own.

terms.label: counterclaim
terms.gloss: A claim a defendant brings against the plaintiff within the same lawsuit, making the defendant a plaintiff on that claim.

terms.label: counteroffer
terms.gloss: A reply to an offer that proposes different terms. It rejects the original offer, which can then no longer be accepted, and makes a new offer in its place.

terms.label: course of dealing
terms.gloss: The pattern of the parties' earlier transactions with each other, which courts use to interpret or fill gaps in their current contract.

terms.label: course of performance
terms.gloss: How the parties have actually carried out this contract on repeated occasions, which courts use as evidence of what its terms mean.

terms.label: cover (UCC § 2-712)
terms.context: \b2[.-]71[1-3]\b|substitute (goods|purchases)|between cover and|cover (price|damages|purchases|and)|proving cover|interest on cover|buyer covered
terms.gloss: A buyer's good-faith purchase of substitute goods after the seller fails to deliver. The buyer may then recover the extra cost over the contract price, plus other proven losses.

terms.label: coverture
terms.gloss: The old common-law rule that a married woman's legal identity merged into her husband's, limiting her power to own property, make contracts, or sue.

terms.label: cracking (gerrymandering)
terms.gloss: Drawing district lines that split a group of voters across several districts so they cannot form a majority anywhere.

terms.label: cross-appeal
terms.gloss: An appeal by the party on the other side of an appeal, asking the higher court to change parts of the decision that went against it.

terms.label: cross-claim
terms.gloss: A claim by one party against a co-party on the same side, such as one defendant suing another defendant, arising from the same events as the original case.

terms.label: cross-complaint
terms.gloss: In California and some other states, a pleading in which a defendant asserts its own claims within the same lawsuit, against the plaintiff, a co-defendant, or a new party.

terms.label: cy pres
terms.gloss: French for "as near as possible": using leftover funds for the next-best purpose, such as giving unclaimed class settlement money to a charity tied to the class's interests.

terms.label: de facto officer doctrine
terms.gloss: A rule treating official acts as valid when done by someone holding an office under apparent authority, even if that person's appointment or election later proves defective.

terms.label: de novo
terms.gloss: Latin for 'anew': a court reviewing a question de novo decides it fresh, giving no deference to the earlier decision.

terms.label: decedent
terms.gloss: A person who has died, especially one whose estate is being settled.

terms.label: declaration (sworn statement)
terms.gloss: A written statement of facts that the signer declares true under penalty of perjury, usable as evidence in place of a sworn affidavit without a notary.

terms.label: declaratory judgment (relief)
terms.gloss: A court ruling that states the parties' legal rights or the meaning of a law or contract, without ordering anyone to pay or act.

terms.label: dedication (of land)
terms.gloss: A landowner's gift of land, or a right to use it, to the public, such as a road, which becomes effective when the government accepts it.

terms.label: deed of trust
terms.gloss: A document pledging real estate as security for a loan, used in some states instead of a mortgage. A neutral trustee can sell the property if the loan goes unpaid.

terms.label: defamation
terms.gloss: A false statement of fact, communicated to others, that harms someone's reputation. Written forms are libel; spoken forms are slander.

terms.label: default judgment
terms.gloss: A judgment entered against a defendant who failed to respond to the lawsuit or otherwise defend it, without a trial on the merits.

terms.label: default rule (gap filler)
terms.gloss: A rule that applies only when the parties, or lawmakers, have not provided otherwise. In contracts, such rules supply terms the agreement leaves open.

terms.label: deficiency (debt)
terms.gloss: The part of a debt still unpaid after the lender takes back and sells the property securing it. A deficiency judgment makes the borrower personally liable for that remainder.

terms.label: demise (lease)
terms.gloss: In property law, a lease or other transfer of the right to possess property for a time. Not death.

terms.label: demurrer
terms.gloss: A response arguing that even if the complaint's facts are true, they give no legal claim. Federal courts replaced it with the motion to dismiss; some states still use it.

terms.label: dependent / independent covenants
terms.gloss: Older terms for how contract promises relate. If dependent, one side must perform before demanding the other's performance; if independent, each must be performed regardless, so either side can sue without performing first.

terms.label: deposition
terms.gloss: Sworn questioning of a witness or party by lawyers outside court before trial, recorded word for word, to gather facts and preserve testimony.

terms.label: derivative suit
terms.gloss: A suit a shareholder brings on the corporation's behalf to enforce the corporation's own rights when its managers will not. Any recovery generally goes to the corporation.

terms.label: detinue
terms.gloss: An old form of lawsuit to recover specific personal property that someone wrongfully keeps, or its value.

terms.label: detrimental reliance
terms.gloss: Reasonably acting, or not acting, in dependence on another's promise in a way that leaves you worse off. It can make a promise enforceable without a bargain (promissory estoppel).

terms.label: devise
terms.gloss: A gift made in a will, traditionally of land or buildings; the person receiving it is the devisee. Modern statutes often use the word for any gift by will.

terms.label: dictum (plural dicta)
terms.gloss: A remark in a judicial opinion that was not needed to decide the case, so later courts are not bound to follow it.

terms.label: diminution in value
terms.gloss: A way to measure damages by how much less the property or result is worth because of the breach, instead of what fixing it would cost.

terms.label: direct-benefit estoppel
terms.gloss: A rule that someone who never signed a contract, but knowingly takes a direct benefit under it, can be held to its terms, such as an arbitration clause.

terms.label: directed verdict
terms.gloss: A judge's ruling that takes a case from the jury and decides it, because the evidence could reasonably support only one result. Federal courts now call it judgment as a matter of law.

terms.label: directory (vs. mandatory)
terms.gloss: Describes a requirement, often a deadline, that officials should follow but whose breach does not invalidate the action taken, unlike a mandatory requirement.

terms.label: disaffirm (a contract)
terms.gloss: To cancel a contract one has a legal right to escape, such as one made as a minor or under duress, by refusing to be bound by it.

terms.label: discharge (of a duty or debt)
terms.gloss: Release from a legal obligation, so the duty to perform or pay no longer exists, whether by performance, agreement, changed circumstances, or a bankruptcy order.

terms.label: discovery (pretrial)
terms.gloss: The formal pretrial process in which each side can require the other to hand over documents and answer questions, including under oath, about the case.

terms.label: disgorgement
terms.gloss: A remedy forcing a wrongdoer to give up the profits gained from the wrong, measured by what the wrongdoer gained rather than what the victim lost.

terms.label: dishonor (of a check)
terms.gloss: A bank's or other payer's refusal to pay a check, note, or similar instrument when it is presented for payment.

terms.label: disparate impact
terms.gloss: Discrimination shown by results: a policy neutral on its face that falls much more heavily on a protected group and lacks enough justification, whatever the intent.

terms.label: dispensing power
terms.gloss: A claimed royal or executive power to excuse people from obeying a statute. England abolished it in 1689, and American courts have held the President has no such power.

terms.label: dispositive
terms.gloss: Decisive: enough by itself to settle a question, or the whole case. A dispositive motion, such as one for summary judgment, seeks to end the case.

terms.label: diversity jurisdiction
terms.gloss: Federal courts' power to hear cases between citizens of different states, or with foreign citizens, when (today) over $75,000 is at stake. Usually no plaintiff may share a state with any defendant.

terms.label: divisible (severable) contract
terms.gloss: A contract that splits into matching pairs of part-performance and part-payment, so completing a part earns its price even if other parts fail. An entire contract must be fully performed.

terms.label: domicile
terms.gloss: A person's legal home: where they live and intend to stay indefinitely. Everyone has exactly one, and it decides which state they are a citizen of for diversity jurisdiction in federal court.

terms.label: donative intent
terms.gloss: A genuine intention to make a gift, needed for a transfer to count as a gift rather than a sale, loan, or bargained exchange.

terms.label: dormant Commerce Clause
terms.gloss: The principle that the Constitution's grant of commerce power to Congress also, on its own, limits state laws that discriminate against or unduly burden interstate trade.

terms.label: dower
terms.gloss: A widow's traditional right to part of her late husband's land, usually a lifetime interest in one-third. Most states have abolished or replaced it.

terms.label: drawee
terms.gloss: The party, usually a bank, that a check or draft orders to pay. The person who writes the order is the drawer; the person paid is the payee.

terms.label: drawer (of a check or bill)
terms.gloss: The person who signs a check or similar written order directing a bank or another party to pay money to someone else.

terms.label: due process
terms.gloss: The Constitution's guarantee that government will not take life, liberty, or property without fair procedures, such as notice and a chance to be heard. It also limits where defendants can be sued.

terms.label: duress
terms.gloss: Wrongful threats or pressure that leave a person no reasonable choice but to agree. A contract made under duress can usually be undone by the pressured party.

terms.label: easement
terms.gloss: A right to use someone else's land for a specific purpose, such as a path or a utility line, without owning it.

terms.label: economic-loss doctrine
terms.gloss: A rule that usually bars tort suits for purely financial losses, such as lost profits or a product's failure to work, leaving those disputes to contract and warranty law.

terms.label: economic waste
terms.gloss: In contract damages, destroying useful work to fix a minor defect. To avoid it, courts may award the drop in value instead of the full cost of rebuilding.

terms.label: effects test
terms.gloss: A basis for a state's courts to hear claims against an out-of-state defendant who intentionally aimed harmful conduct at the state, knowing the injury would be felt there.

terms.label: efficient breach
terms.gloss: The theory that breaking a contract and paying the other side's damages can be better overall when performing would cost more than it is worth.

terms.label: ejectment
terms.gloss: A traditional lawsuit to recover possession of land from someone occupying it, establishing the right to possess it.

terms.label: ejusdem generis
terms.gloss: Latin for 'of the same kind': a reading rule that general words following a list cover only things similar to the listed items.

terms.label: eminent domain
terms.gloss: The government's power to take private property for public use, so long as it pays the owner just compensation.

terms.label: en banc
terms.gloss: Decided by all the active judges of a court (or a large panel of them) together, instead of the usual three-judge panel, usually for especially important or conflicting questions.

terms.label: encumbrance
terms.gloss: A claim or right in property held by someone other than the owner, such as a mortgage, lien, or easement, that limits the owner's use or sale of it.

terms.label: endorsement (indorsement)
terms.gloss: A signature on a check or note, usually on the back, that transfers it to someone else or makes the signer liable to pay if the main party does not.

terms.label: endorsement (insurance)
terms.gloss: In insurance, a written amendment added to a policy that changes its coverage, such as adding a vehicle or an exclusion.

terms.label: enjoin
terms.gloss: To forbid someone, by a court order called an injunction, from doing something (or, less often, to require them to do it).

terms.label: equally divided court
terms.gloss: A tie vote among the judges. The lower court's decision stands, but the tie explains no reasoning and sets no precedent.

terms.label: equitable estoppel
terms.gloss: A rule barring a party from asserting a right when its own words or conduct led another person to reasonably rely on the opposite, to that person's harm.

terms.label: equitable ownership
terms.gloss: Having the real benefit of property, protected by courts of equity, while someone else holds legal title, as a buyer under a signed purchase contract does before closing.

terms.label: equitable relief
terms.gloss: A court order to do or stop doing something, such as an injunction or specific performance, rather than an award of money damages.

terms.label: balance of equities
terms.gloss: The comparative fairness and hardship to each side that a court weighs when deciding whether to grant an injunction, specific performance, or a similar order.

terms.label: equity (courts of equity)
terms.gloss: The body of law, from England's old chancery courts, that offers remedies like injunctions and specific performance when money damages would not be enough. Not fairness or ownership value.

terms.label: Erie doctrine
terms.gloss: The rule that federal courts deciding state-law claims apply state substantive law but federal procedure. Deciding which category a rule falls into is the 'Erie question.'

terms.label: escheat
terms.gloss: The passing of property to the state when its owner dies with no will and no heirs to inherit it, or when property such as a bank account is abandoned.

terms.label: escrow
terms.gloss: An arrangement in which a neutral third party holds money or documents until agreed conditions are met, then releases them.

terms.label: estoppel
terms.gloss: A rule barring a party from taking a position that contradicts its own earlier words, conduct, or a prior ruling, when others relied on it.

terms.label: ex parte
terms.gloss: Done at the request of one side without notice to, or participation by, the other side, such as an emergency order issued after hearing only one party.

terms.label: ex post facto law
terms.gloss: Latin for 'after the fact.' The Constitution forbids criminal laws that punish conduct that was legal when done, or that increase its punishment afterward.

terms.label: exaction
terms.gloss: A charge the government demands, such as a tax or duty. In land-use law, a condition attached to a building permit, such as giving land or paying a fee.

terms.label: exclusionary rule
terms.gloss: The rule that evidence the government obtains by violating a person's constitutional rights, such as through an illegal search, generally cannot be used against that person at a criminal trial.

terms.label: exculpatory
terms.gloss: Tending to clear someone of blame. Exculpatory evidence points toward innocence; an exculpatory clause releases a party in advance from liability for certain harms.

terms.label: excusable neglect
terms.gloss: A good enough reason for missing a deadline, such as an honest mistake, that lets a court allow a late filing or undo a default. Courts weigh the reason, delay, good faith, and harm to the other side.

terms.label: execution (of a judgment)
terms.gloss: The court-ordered process of enforcing a money judgment, for example by having a sheriff seize and sell the losing party's property to pay it.

terms.label: executory
terms.gloss: Not yet performed: a promise or contract on which some performance still remains to be done.

terms.label: exhaustion of remedies
terms.gloss: The requirement to use every available step within an agency or grievance system before going to court. Not tiredness.

terms.label: expectation damages
terms.gloss: Money that puts the injured party where it would have been if the contract had been performed: roughly the value of the lost bargain, minus any costs it saved by not performing.

terms.label: presumption against extraterritoriality
terms.gloss: The presumption that a federal statute applies only within the United States unless Congress clearly indicates it should reach conduct or events abroad.

terms.label: extrinsic evidence
terms.gloss: Evidence from outside a written document, such as negotiations or trade practice, used to show what its words mean.

terms.label: facial challenge
terms.gloss: A claim that a law or contract term is invalid in every application, on its face, rather than only as applied to the challenger's own situation.

terms.label: fact pleading (code pleading)
terms.gloss: An older pleading system, still used in some states, requiring a complaint to state the facts making up each element of a claim, rather than legal conclusions or a short general statement.

terms.label: failure of consideration
terms.gloss: A defense that arises when the performance promised in exchange never happens or becomes worthless, which can excuse the other side from performing or paying.

terms.label: failure to state a claim
terms.gloss: Stating a claim means alleging facts that, if true, would give the plaintiff a legal right to relief. A complaint that fails to do so can be dismissed without a trial.

terms.label: fair play and substantial justice
terms.gloss: The fairness standard from International Shoe: suing an out-of-state defendant in a state must be reasonable, not merely supported by minimum contacts, weighing the burdens and interests involved.

terms.label: fairness hearing
terms.gloss: A court hearing where affected people may object before the judge decides whether a proposed class-action settlement or consent decree is fair, reasonable, and adequate.

terms.label: federal common law
terms.gloss: Rules made by federal judges, not by statutes, in the few areas where national interests need one uniform federal rule.

terms.label: federal-question jurisdiction
terms.gloss: A question of federal law. Federal courts have 'federal-question jurisdiction' over cases arising under the Constitution, federal statutes, or treaties, usually because federal law creates the plaintiff's claim.

terms.label: fee simple
terms.gloss: The fullest form of land ownership: the owner holds it indefinitely and may sell it, give it away, or pass it on at death.

terms.label: fiduciary duty
terms.gloss: The duty of loyalty and care owed by a fiduciary: someone trusted to act for another, such as a trustee, agent, partner, or director, who must put the other's interests first.

terms.label: final agency action
terms.gloss: An agency decision ready for court challenge under the Administrative Procedure Act: it ends the agency's decisionmaking and determines rights or carries legal consequences.

terms.label: final-judgment rule
terms.gloss: The general rule that a party may appeal only after the trial court finishes the whole case, not from each ruling along the way.

terms.label: firm offer
terms.gloss: A definite offer that can be accepted to form a contract, not just an invitation to negotiate. Under the UCC, a merchant's signed written promise to keep an offer open binds for up to three months.

terms.label: question of first impression
terms.gloss: A legal question that no court in that jurisdiction has decided before, so there is no binding earlier decision to follow.

terms.label: fitness for review (ripeness)
terms.gloss: Part of the ripeness test: whether an issue is concrete and settled enough for a court to decide now, without waiting for further facts or agency action.

terms.label: f.o.b. (free on board)
terms.gloss: A shipping term naming the place, such as the seller's plant or a ship, up to which the seller bears delivery costs and risk of loss; after that, the buyer does.

terms.label: forbearance
terms.gloss: Deliberately holding back from doing something one has a right to do, such as suing or collecting a debt. In contracts, that holding back can be the price paid for a promise.

terms.label: force majeure
terms.gloss: A contract term excusing or delaying performance when an extraordinary event beyond the parties' control, such as war or natural disaster, prevents it.

terms.label: foreign corporation
terms.gloss: A corporation formed under the laws of a different state or country from the one where it is doing business or being sued. It need not be foreign to the U.S.

terms.label: formal rulemaking
terms.gloss: Agency rule-writing done through trial-like hearings on the record, required only when a statute says so; most rules use the simpler notice-and-comment process.

terms.label: forms of action
terms.gloss: The fixed categories of old common-law lawsuits, such as trespass, debt, or assumpsit. Each had its own writ and procedure, and choosing the wrong one could defeat a claim.

terms.label: forum-defendant rule
terms.gloss: The rule that a case cannot be moved from state to federal court on diversity grounds if a properly joined and served defendant is a citizen of the state where it was filed.

terms.label: law of the forum (lex fori)
terms.gloss: The law of the place where the court hearing the case sits, as opposed to the law of another state or country connected to the dispute.

terms.label: forum non conveniens
terms.gloss: Latin for 'inconvenient forum': a court's power to dismiss a case it could hear because a court elsewhere, often abroad, is a much more suitable place for it.

terms.label: forum-selection clause
terms.gloss: A contract term choosing the court or place where the parties' disputes must be litigated. Courts usually enforce it unless enforcement would be unreasonable or unjust.

terms.label: fraud on the court
terms.gloss: Misconduct that corrupts the court process itself, such as fabricated evidence or bribing a judge, rather than just deceiving the other side. It permits reopening even old judgments.

terms.label: suppression (fraudulent concealment)
terms.gloss: A fraud claim for hiding, or failing to disclose, an important fact one had a duty to reveal, causing the other person harm.

terms.label: front pay
terms.gloss: Money for wages a wrongly fired or excluded worker will lose in the future, awarded instead of putting the worker back in the job.

terms.label: frustration of purpose
terms.gloss: A contract excuse: an unexpected event destroys the deal's main purpose, known to both sides, so duties end though performance remains possible. In English law, frustration also covers impossibility.

terms.label: full faith and credit
terms.gloss: The constitutional and statutory duty of each state, and of federal courts, to honor the laws, official records, and court judgments of other states.

terms.label: future interest
terms.gloss: A legal interest held now in property that gives the right to possess it only later, for example after someone else's life estate ends. Some depend on a condition and may never take effect.

terms.label: garnishment
terms.gloss: A court process that collects a debt from money or property a third party holds for the debtor, such as wages owed by an employer (the garnishee).

terms.label: general appearance
terms.gloss: Taking part in a case in a way that accepts the court's power over you, which usually gives up objections to personal jurisdiction.

terms.label: general damages
terms.gloss: Damages for harm that naturally follows from the kind of wrong done, which anyone so wronged would suffer. Unlike special damages, they need not be specifically pleaded.

terms.label: general denial
terms.gloss: An answer that denies every allegation in the complaint at once rather than responding to each one separately.

terms.label: general issue (plea)
terms.gloss: In common-law pleading, a defendant's blanket denial of the plaintiff's whole claim, which let the defendant contest everything at trial.

terms.label: general jurisdiction (over a defendant)
terms.gloss: A court's power over a defendant for any claim at all, even one unrelated to the state. For a person, usually their home state; for a company, where it is incorporated or headquartered.

terms.label: general verdict
terms.gloss: A jury verdict that simply names the winner and any amount awarded, without stating the jury's findings on the specific disputed issues.

terms.label: generalized grievance
terms.gloss: A complaint about government shared equally by all citizens, such as an interest in lawful government, which alone does not give anyone the right to sue in federal court.

terms.label: genuine dispute of material fact
terms.context: \b(summary judgment|summary-judgment|rule 56|trial|factfinder|material facts?|jury|no genuine|raising a genuine|raised a genuine|found a genuine|remained|triable|no-genuine-dispute)\b
terms.gloss: A real disagreement, backed by evidence, about a fact that could change the outcome. If one exists, the court cannot grant summary judgment on that issue; a trial must resolve it.

terms.label: governmental immunity
terms.gloss: A government's protection from being sued or held liable without its consent. The term is often used for local governments such as cities and counties.

terms.label: gratuitous
terms.gloss: Given or promised for nothing in return. In contract law such a promise usually cannot be enforced, though reasonable reliance on it sometimes changes that.

terms.label: gravamen
terms.gloss: The core or most important part of a claim or complaint: what it is really about.

terms.label: guardian ad litem
terms.gloss: A person a court appoints to protect the interests of a child or an incapacitated person within a particular lawsuit.

terms.label: habeas corpus
terms.gloss: A court order requiring the government to bring a detained person before a judge and justify the detention; also the lawsuit asking for that order.

terms.label: hard-look review
terms.gloss: Careful court review of whether an agency seriously examined the relevant data, alternatives, and objections and explained its choice, rather than acting arbitrarily.

terms.label: harmless error
terms.gloss: A trial mistake that an appeals court finds did not affect the outcome, so it is no reason to reverse the judgment.

terms.label: hearsay
terms.gloss: An out-of-court statement offered in court to prove that what it says is true. It is generally excluded as evidence unless an exception applies.

terms.label: heightened scrutiny (intermediate / exacting)
terms.gloss: A middle level of court review, stricter than rational basis: the government must show the law serves an important interest and is substantially related to it.

terms.label: holder in due course
terms.gloss: Someone who took a check, note, or other negotiable instrument in good faith and for value, without notice of problems with it. Such a holder can enforce it despite most defenses.

terms.label: holding (of a court)
terms.gloss: The legal ruling a court's decision actually rests on, which binds later cases, as opposed to side remarks (dicta) not needed for the result.

terms.label: illusory promise
terms.gloss: A promise that commits the promisor to nothing because it leaves them free to do whatever they like, so it cannot serve as consideration.

terms.label: impeachment (of a witness or verdict)
terms.gloss: Attacking the believability of a witness or the validity of a verdict, for example by showing contradictions or bias. Here it does not mean removing a public official.

terms.label: impleader
terms.gloss: A defendant's bringing a new party, the third-party defendant, into the suit, claiming that party must repay some or all of what the defendant may owe the plaintiff.

terms.label: implied contract (implied in fact)
terms.gloss: A real contract shown by the parties' conduct and the circumstances rather than by spoken or written words.

terms.label: implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing
match: implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing
covenant of good faith and fair dealing
duty of good faith and fair dealing
terms.gloss: A duty the law reads into nearly every contract: neither side may act to unfairly deprive the other of the deal's expected benefits, even without breaking an express term.

terms.label: implied repeal
terms.gloss: The disfavored idea that a later statute silently cancels an earlier one. Courts accept it only when the two truly cannot both operate.

terms.label: implied warranty
terms.gloss: A guarantee about goods that the law reads into a sale automatically, even if the seller never stated it, such as that the goods are fit for ordinary use.

terms.label: implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose
match: warranty of fitness for a particular purpose
terms.gloss: A guarantee, read into a sale by law, that goods will suit the buyer's particular purpose. It arises when the seller knows that purpose and that the buyer relies on the seller's judgment.

terms.label: impossibility
terms.gloss: A defense excusing a party from performing when an unforeseen event, such as destruction of the subject matter, makes performance objectively impossible.

terms.label: impracticability
terms.gloss: A defense excusing contract performance when an unexpected event, not the party's fault, makes performing far more difficult or costly than anyone assumed.

terms.label: impressment
terms.gloss: Forcing a person into naval or military service against their will. Britain's navy historically seized merchant sailors this way, taking them away from the ship they had signed on to serve.

terms.label: improper (fraudulent) joinder
terms.gloss: A doctrine letting a federal court ignore a defendant named to block removal, often one from the plaintiff's own state, when the plaintiff has no reasonable claim against it, so the case stays in federal court.

terms.label: in camera
terms.gloss: Latin for 'in chambers': privately, by the judge alone, as when a judge reads sensitive documents without showing them to the public or the other side.

terms.label: in personam
terms.gloss: Latin for 'against the person': a case or judgment that binds a particular person, which requires personal jurisdiction over them, rather than one about rights in specific property.

terms.label: in rem
terms.gloss: Latin for 'against the thing': a proceeding or jurisdiction aimed at property itself, deciding everyone's rights in it, rather than at a person.

terms.label: incidental beneficiary
terms.gloss: Someone who would gain from a contract between other people but whom the parties did not mean to benefit, so that person has no right to enforce it.

terms.label: incidental damages
terms.gloss: Reasonable extra costs a party incurs in dealing with a breach, such as inspecting, storing, shipping back, or reselling rejected goods.

terms.label: inculpatory
terms.gloss: Tending to show that a person is guilty of a crime or responsible for a wrong. The opposite is exculpatory.

terms.label: indemnity
terms.gloss: A promise or duty to cover another person's losses or legal liability, for example by paying a claim brought against that person.

terms.label: indenture
terms.gloss: A formal written contract, especially one setting the terms of a bond or note issue and naming a trustee to protect the investors.

terms.label: independent agency
terms.gloss: A federal agency, such as the FTC, whose leaders Congress has protected from removal by the President except for cause. How far Congress may do this is disputed.

terms.label: indispensable (required) party
terms.gloss: A person whose interests are so bound up in a lawsuit that they must be added if possible; if they cannot be, the court may dismiss rather than go on without them (federal Rule 19).

terms.label: infancy (being a minor)
terms.gloss: Not babyhood: being under the legal age of adulthood, usually 18. A minor can generally cancel contracts made while underage, but must still pay fair value for necessities received.

terms.label: inferior officer / principal officer
terms.gloss: Officers of the United States exercise significant federal power. Principal officers answer only to the President and need Senate confirmation; inferior officers are supervised by other officers and can be appointed more simply.

terms.label: informal (notice-and-comment) rulemaking
terms.gloss: The usual way federal agencies make regulations: publishing a proposed rule, taking written public comments, and issuing a final rule with an explanation, with no trial-like hearing.

terms.label: on information and belief
terms.gloss: A phrase in pleadings meaning the person asserts a fact as true based on what they have been told and believe, not on firsthand knowledge.

terms.label: injunction
terms.gloss: A court order requiring someone to do, or more often to stop doing, a particular thing.

terms.label: injunctive relief
terms.gloss: A court order requiring someone to do, or stop doing, something, as opposed to an award of money. Courts usually grant it only when money could not adequately fix the harm.

terms.label: injury in fact
terms.gloss: The first requirement for standing (the right to sue in federal court): a concrete harm to the plaintiff personally that is actual or imminent, not hypothetical or a grievance everyone shares.

terms.label: instrument (legal document)
terms.gloss: A formal written legal document, such as a contract, deed, will, or promissory note. A negotiable instrument is a signed paper promising or ordering payment, like a check.

terms.label: integration clause (merger clause)
terms.gloss: An integrated writing is one the parties meant as their final agreement, so earlier or side deals cannot contradict it (or, if fully integrated, add to it). An integration or merger clause says so.

terms.label: intelligible principle
terms.gloss: The test for a delegation of power: a statute is valid if Congress gives a guiding principle clear enough to direct and limit the agency acting under it.

terms.label: intended beneficiary
terms.gloss: A third person whom the contracting parties meant to benefit, who can therefore sue to enforce the contract. An incidental beneficiary cannot.

terms.label: intentional infliction of emotional distress
terms.gloss: A claim for severe emotional harm caused by extreme and outrageous conduct done intentionally or recklessly.

terms.label: intentional tort
terms.gloss: A civil wrong done on purpose, such as battery, assault, or trespass, as opposed to harm caused by carelessness.

terms.label: inter partes
terms.gloss: Latin for 'between the parties': a proceeding in which both opposing sides take part, such as a challenge to an issued patent argued by both sides before the Patent and Trademark Office.

terms.label: inter vivos
terms.gloss: Latin for 'between the living': a gift, transfer, or trust made during the owner's lifetime, as opposed to by will at death.

terms.label: interim final rule
terms.gloss: A regulation an agency makes effective without first taking public comment, usually citing good cause such as urgency, while inviting comments afterward.

terms.label: interlocutory
terms.gloss: Made during a lawsuit, before the final judgment. An interlocutory appeal is an appeal of such a mid-case ruling, usually allowed only in limited situations.

terms.label: interpleader
match: bill in the nature of interpleader
terms.gloss: A suit in which someone holding money or property that several people claim brings all the claimants into one case, so the court decides who is entitled to it.

terms.label: interpretive rule
terms.gloss: An agency statement explaining how it reads an existing statute or regulation. It lacks the force of law, so the agency may issue it without first taking public comment.

terms.label: interrogatories
terms.gloss: Written questions one party in a lawsuit sends another party before trial, which must be answered in writing and under oath.

terms.label: interstate compact
terms.gloss: A binding agreement between states, usually approved by Congress. Once approved, it also counts as federal law, and courts enforce its terms like a contract.

terms.label: intervention
terms.gloss: An outsider's entry into a lawsuit already under way, joining as a party to protect its own stake in the outcome. Courts allow it either as of right or by permission.

terms.label: intestate
terms.gloss: Without a valid will. When someone dies without one, state law decides who inherits the property.

terms.label: intrusion on seclusion
terms.gloss: A privacy wrong: intentionally intruding, physically or electronically, into someone's private affairs in a way a reasonable person would find highly offensive.

terms.label: inverse condemnation
terms.gloss: A suit by a property owner claiming the government effectively took or damaged the property without a formal condemnation proceeding, asking to be paid for it.

terms.label: irreparable harm
terms.gloss: Harm that money awarded later could not adequately make up for. Showing it is usually required to get an injunction.

terms.label: issue (descendants)
terms.gloss: In wills and inheritance, a person's descendants: children, grandchildren, and later generations. To die "without issue" is to leave no descendants.

terms.label: issue preclusion (collateral estoppel)
terms.gloss: A bar on relitigating a specific question of fact or law that was actually litigated, decided, and essential to an earlier final judgment. Also called collateral estoppel.

terms.label: preservation (for appeal)
terms.gloss: Raising an objection or argument properly and on time in the lower court so an appeals court will consider it. An 'unpreserved' point is usually treated as given up.

terms.label: joinder
terms.gloss: Bringing additional parties or claims into one lawsuit so related disputes are decided together. Court rules say when it is allowed and when an absent party must be added.

terms.label: joint and several liability
terms.gloss: Shared liability where each responsible party can be made to pay the whole amount, leaving them to sort out their shares among themselves.

terms.label: joint tenancy
terms.gloss: Shared ownership of property in which, when one owner dies, that owner's share passes automatically to the surviving owners rather than through the deceased owner's will or estate.

terms.label: judgment absolute
terms.gloss: A final judgment ending the case with no new trial. Under old New York practice, appealing an order granting a new trial required agreeing to final judgment against oneself if the order was affirmed.

terms.label: judgment as a matter of law
match: judgments as a matter of law
judgment as a matter of law
terms.gloss: A ruling by the judge, during or after a jury trial, that no reasonable jury could find for the other side, so the judge decides the case instead of the jury or despite its verdict.

terms.label: judgment notwithstanding the verdict (JNOV)
match: motion for judgment notwithstanding the verdict
terms.gloss: A judge's ruling overriding a jury's verdict because no reasonable jury could have reached it on the evidence. Federal courts now call this judgment as a matter of law.

terms.label: judgment on the pleadings
match: motion for judgment on the pleadings
terms.gloss: A ruling, under Federal Rule 12(c) or a state equivalent, deciding the case from the complaint and answer alone because, accepting the facts they allege, one side is entitled to win as a matter of law.

terms.label: judicial estoppel
terms.gloss: A rule barring a party who persuaded a court to accept one position from later taking a clearly inconsistent position to gain an unfair advantage.

terms.label: judicial notice
terms.gloss: A court's acceptance of a fact as true without formal proof, because it is common knowledge or easily confirmed from reliable sources.

terms.label: jury charge
terms.context: departure from the charge|under (that|the) charge|charge rulings|charge’s adequacy|jury charge|charge to the jury|judge’s charge
terms.gloss: The judge's instructions to the jury explaining the law it must apply to the facts. Not a criminal accusation.

terms.label: justiciability
terms.gloss: Whether a dispute is the kind a court may decide at all: a real, current controversy suited to judicial resolution, brought by a proper party.

terms.label: knockout rule (UCC § 2-207)
terms.gloss: The majority approach when two businesses' forms contain conflicting terms under UCC § 2-207: the clashing terms cancel out, and the Code's default terms fill the gap.

terms.label: laches
terms.gloss: A defense that bars a claim for an equitable remedy when the plaintiff waited unreasonably long to sue and the delay harmed the defendant.

terms.label: law of the case
terms.gloss: The practice that a legal ruling made earlier in a case, especially by an appeals court, generally governs the rest of that same case.

terms.label: leave (of court)
terms.gloss: A court's permission to take a procedural step, such as amending a complaint or filing an appeal. 'Without leave to amend' means the plaintiff may not try again.

terms.label: legacy
terms.gloss: A gift of money or other personal property left to someone in a will.

terms.label: legal-certainty test
terms.gloss: The test for whether a case meets the minimum amount in dispute for federal court: the plaintiff's good-faith claim controls unless it is legally certain the plaintiff could not recover that much.

terms.label: legal detriment
terms.gloss: Doing something one had a legal right not to do, or refraining from something one could lawfully do. It can count as consideration even without actual harm.

terms.label: legatee
terms.gloss: A person who receives property under a will. A residuary legatee takes whatever is left after the specific gifts, debts, and expenses are paid.

terms.label: legislative rule
terms.gloss: An agency regulation with the force of law, binding the public like a statute. It usually must first go through public notice and comment. Agencies, not legislatures, make it.

terms.label: legislative veto
terms.gloss: A device letting Congress, one chamber, or a committee cancel an executive action by resolution, without passing a new law. The Supreme Court held it unconstitutional in INS v. Chadha (1983).

terms.label: levy (of execution)
terms.gloss: An officer's seizure of a debtor's property under court authority, so it can be sold to pay a judgment. Not a tax.

terms.label: libel (admiralty)
terms.gloss: In admiralty (maritime) courts, the pleading that starts a case, like a complaint, often against a ship or cargo itself; its filer is the libelant. Unrelated to defamation.

terms.label: liberal construction
terms.gloss: Reading a rule, statute, or document generously to carry out its purpose, rather than strictly by the narrowest meaning of its words.

terms.label: liberty interest
terms.gloss: A freedom protected by the Due Process Clauses, such as freedom from physical restraint, so the government must use fair procedures before taking it away.

terms.label: liberty of contract
terms.gloss: An early-1900s constitutional doctrine, abandoned in 1937, that treated freedom to bargain as protected liberty. Courts used it to strike down many wage, hour, and labor laws.

terms.label: lien
terms.gloss: A creditor's legal claim against property as security for a debt, which can let the creditor have it sold if the debt is not paid.

terms.label: life estate
terms.gloss: A right to own and use property only for the rest of a particular person's life, after which it passes to someone else.

terms.label: limited fund (class action)
terms.gloss: A pool of money, such as an insurance policy, too small to pay all claims in full. It can justify one class action binding every claimant, with no opt-outs.

terms.label: limited jurisdiction
terms.gloss: Describes courts, like all federal courts, that may hear only the kinds of cases the Constitution and statutes allow them to hear.

terms.label: limiting instruction
terms.gloss: A judge's direction telling the jury it may use certain evidence only for one stated purpose and must ignore it for others.

terms.label: liquidated claim (vs. unliquidated)
terms.gloss: A liquidated claim is for a fixed, definite sum of money. An unliquidated claim, such as one for personal injuries, has an amount a court or jury must still set.

terms.label: liquidated damages
terms.gloss: Damages for breach set in the contract in advance. Courts enforce them if they were a reasonable estimate of the likely harm; otherwise they are an unenforceable penalty.

terms.label: lis pendens
terms.gloss: A notice filed in public land records that a pending lawsuit claims an interest in a property, warning later buyers or lenders that they take it subject to the outcome.

terms.label: lodestar
terms.gloss: The usual starting figure for a court-awarded attorney fee: reasonable hours worked times a reasonable hourly rate, which the court may then raise or lower.

terms.label: logical outgrowth
terms.gloss: The test for whether an agency's final rule may differ from its proposal: the change must be one commenters could reasonably have anticipated from what was proposed.

terms.label: long-arm statute
terms.gloss: A state law letting its courts reach defendants outside the state, based on their in-state conduct, such as doing business or causing injury there.

terms.label: loss of consortium
terms.gloss: A claim by an injured or killed person's spouse, or sometimes family, for the companionship, affection, and help lost because of the injury.

terms.label: mailbox rule
terms.gloss: The default contract rule that a properly mailed acceptance takes effect when it is sent, not when it arrives.

terms.label: major questions doctrine
terms.gloss: The rule that courts will not read a statute as giving an agency power over matters of vast economic or political significance unless Congress clearly authorized it.

terms.label: mandamus
terms.gloss: A court order commanding a government official or lower court to carry out a clear legal duty. Courts grant it only in extraordinary cases.

terms.label: mandate (appellate)
terms.gloss: An appeals court's formal order sending its decision to the lower court, ending the appeal and directing what happens next.
