terms.label: marketable title
terms.gloss: Ownership of land free from reasonable doubt, such as hidden claims, liens, or defects, so that a reasonably careful buyer would accept it.

terms.label: Marks rule
terms.gloss: A rule for reading a splintered Supreme Court decision with no majority opinion: the holding is the position of the Justices who concurred on the narrowest grounds.

terms.label: master (special master)
terms.gloss: A person a court appoints to help with part of a case, such as taking evidence, calculating losses, or supervising a settlement, and reporting back to the judge.

terms.label: material alteration (UCC § 2-207)
terms.gloss: Under the UCC's battle-of-the-forms rule, an added term in a reply form that would cause unfair surprise or hardship. Between merchants, such a term does not join the contract.

terms.label: material breach
terms.gloss: A failure to perform so serious that it defeats the main purpose of the deal, letting the other side stop performing and sue.

terms.label: Mathews balancing test
terms.gloss: The test for how much procedure due process requires: weigh the private interest, the risk of error and the value of added safeguards, and the government's burden.

terms.label: as a matter of law
terms.gloss: Decided by applying legal rules alone, because the facts are undisputed or no reasonable factfinder could see them otherwise, so no jury question remains.

terms.label: mechanic's lien
terms.gloss: A legal claim against property by a builder or supplier who improved it and was not paid, which can be enforced by forcing a sale.

terms.label: mend the hold
terms.gloss: A doctrine, mainly in Illinois, limiting a party who gave one reason for refusing to perform from switching to a different reason once sued.

terms.label: merchant (UCC)
terms.gloss: Under the UCC, a person who deals in goods of the kind involved or holds out special knowledge of them. Some sales rules apply only to merchants or between merchants.

terms.label: implied warranty of merchantability
terms.gloss: A merchant seller's automatic guarantee that goods are fit for their ordinary purpose and of acceptable quality in the trade. 'Merchantable' goods meet that standard.

terms.label: merger of law and equity
terms.gloss: The combining of the once-separate court systems for law (money damages, juries) and equity (injunctions, no jury) into one civil action, done in federal courts by the 1938 Federal Rules.
terms.context: \b(equity|equitable|law action|jury right|jury guarantee|rule 38|rules enabling act|historical jury)\b

terms.label: merits
terms.gloss: The substance of a dispute: which side should win under the facts and the law, as opposed to side questions such as jurisdiction, timing, or procedure.

terms.label: mesne profits
terms.gloss: Damages a landowner recovers from someone who wrongfully occupied the land, measured by the rent or profits the land would have produced during that occupation.

terms.label: metes and bounds
terms.gloss: A way of describing land by its boundary lines, using measured distances and compass directions from landmarks.

terms.label: minimum contacts
terms.gloss: The connections a defendant must have with a state before that state's courts can fairly exercise power over the defendant under the Due Process Clause.

terms.label: ministerial (duty)
terms.gloss: Describing a duty the law spells out so exactly that the official has no choice about whether or how to perform it. Courts can order such acts done.

terms.label: misjoinder
terms.gloss: Wrongly combining parties or claims in one lawsuit when the rules do not allow them to be joined together.

terms.label: mitigation (of damages)
terms.gloss: An injured party's duty to take reasonable steps to limit its losses after a breach or injury, such as seeking other work. Losses it could have avoided are not recoverable.

terms.label: mixed question of law and fact
match: mixed questions of law and fact
mixed question of law and fact
terms.gloss: An issue that requires applying a legal standard to the facts, such as whether conduct was reasonable. How much appeals courts defer depends on whether it is mainly factual or legal.

terms.label: money had and received
terms.gloss: An old common-law claim to recover money the defendant holds that in fairness belongs to the plaintiff, such as a payment made by mistake or for something never delivered.

terms.label: moot
terms.gloss: No longer a live dispute: events have settled the issue or a ruling could make no practical difference, so courts usually decline to decide it.

terms.label: moral obligation
terms.gloss: A duty of conscience, such as gratitude for a past kindness, that the law does not enforce alone. Some courts enforce a later promise to pay for a benefit already received.

terms.label: more definite statement
terms.gloss: A request that the court order the other side to redo a pleading so vague or ambiguous that a fair response cannot reasonably be prepared.

terms.label: mortgagee
terms.gloss: The lender in a mortgage, who holds an interest in the property as security for the loan; the borrower is the mortgagor.

terms.label: motion to compel
terms.gloss: A request that a court order the other side to do something, most often to take the dispute to arbitration under their agreement, or to hand over requested information.

terms.label: motion to dismiss
terms.gloss: A request that the court end a lawsuit early, without a trial, for example because the complaint fails to state a legal claim or the court lacks power over the case.

terms.label: motion to quash
terms.gloss: A request that a court set aside or void something, such as defective service of process, a subpoena, or a charge. 'Quashed' means annulled.

terms.label: motion to strike
terms.gloss: A request that the court delete material from a pleading or the record, such as an improper allegation, defense, or piece of evidence, so it no longer counts.

terms.label: motion to suppress
terms.gloss: A request that the court exclude certain evidence from trial, most often a criminal defendant's claim that the government obtained it unlawfully.

terms.label: movant
terms.gloss: The party asking the court for the ruling now being decided; the party opposing that request is the nonmovant.

terms.label: multidistrict litigation (MDL)
terms.gloss: A federal procedure that transfers similar cases filed in different districts to one judge for combined pretrial work, such as discovery, before sending any unresolved ones back for trial.

terms.label: municipal corporation
terms.gloss: A city, town, or village organized as a legal body to run local government. Not a business.

terms.label: mutual mistake
terms.gloss: Both parties sharing the same wrong belief about a basic fact the deal rests on, which can let the disadvantaged party undo the contract unless it bore that risk.

terms.label: mutuality of obligation
terms.gloss: The older idea that both sides must be bound or neither is. Modern law asks only whether there is consideration; if there is, nothing more is needed.

terms.label: mutuality (in preclusion)
terms.gloss: The older rule that only someone who would have been bound by a prior judgment, normally a party to that case, could use it against an opponent later.

terms.label: necessaries
terms.gloss: Basic needs such as food, shelter, clothing, and medical care. A minor must pay their fair value even without a binding contract; traditionally a wife could buy them on her husband's credit.

terms.label: Necessary and Proper Clause
terms.gloss: The constitutional provision letting Congress pass laws reasonably suited to carrying out its listed powers, even when the law itself is not one of those powers.

terms.label: negligence per se
terms.gloss: Negligence established by the defendant's unexcused violation of a safety statute or regulation meant to protect people like the injured person.

terms.label: negligent misrepresentation
terms.gloss: Carelessly supplying false information that someone justifiably relies on in a business or financial decision, causing loss. Unlike fraud, it requires no intent to deceive.

terms.label: negotiable instrument
terms.gloss: A signed written unconditional promise or order to pay a fixed sum, such as a check or promissory note, that can be transferred to others, who may then enforce it.

terms.label: next friend
terms.gloss: A person, often a parent, who brings a suit on behalf of someone who cannot sue alone, such as a child or a detained person, without becoming a party.

terms.label: nominal damages
terms.gloss: A token sum, often one dollar, awarded when a legal right was violated but no real financial loss was proved.

terms.label: nondelegation doctrine
terms.gloss: The constitutional principle that Congress may not hand its lawmaking power to agencies or others; it must set the basic policy and limits itself.

terms.label: nonmutual preclusion (offensive / defensive)
terms.gloss: Use of an earlier judgment against the party that lost it by someone who was not in that case. Offensive use helps a new plaintiff win; defensive use helps a new defendant.

terms.label: nonsuit
terms.gloss: Ending a lawsuit without deciding who is right, because the plaintiff dropped it or failed to offer enough proof. The plaintiff can often sue again.

terms.label: noscitur a sociis
terms.gloss: Latin for 'known by its companions': a reading rule that an unclear word in a list takes meaning from the words around it.

terms.label: notice-and-comment rulemaking
terms.gloss: The usual way a federal agency makes binding rules (APA § 553): it publishes notice of a proposed rule, takes public comments, considers them, and explains the final rule.

terms.label: notice by publication
terms.gloss: Giving legal notice by printing it in a newspaper. Under Mullane, it suffices only for people who cannot reasonably be found; known people need mail or similar direct notice.

terms.label: notice of proposed rulemaking
terms.gloss: An agency's public announcement, in the Federal Register, of a rule it is considering, describing it and inviting written comments before it becomes final.

terms.label: novation
terms.gloss: A new agreement, accepted by everyone involved, that replaces an existing one, often by substituting a new party, and releases the original obligation.

terms.label: numerosity (Rule 23(a)(1))
terms.gloss: The class-action requirement that the class be so large that bringing in every member as a named party would be impracticable.

terms.label: nunc pro tunc
terms.gloss: Latin for 'now for then': a court order given effect as of an earlier date, usually to correct the record or reflect what already happened.

terms.label: obligor and obligee
terms.gloss: The obligor is the party who owes a payment or other duty; the obligee is the party entitled to receive it.

terms.label: occupy the field (field preemption)
terms.gloss: For federal law to regulate a subject so completely that it leaves no room for state law there, displacing even state rules that do not directly conflict with it.

terms.label: offer of proof
terms.gloss: A lawyer's explanation, made outside the jury's hearing, of what excluded evidence would have shown, so an appeals court can judge whether excluding it was harmful.

terms.label: official capacity
terms.gloss: Acting, or being sued, as the holder of a government office rather than as a private person. An official-capacity suit is in effect against the office itself, not the officer personally.

terms.label: on-the-record requirement (APA)
terms.gloss: A statute's direction that an agency decide 'on the record after' a hearing. It triggers formal, trial-like APA procedures under sections 556 and 557; without it, simpler procedures usually suffice.

terms.label: order to show cause
terms.gloss: A court order requiring a party to appear and explain why the court should not take a proposed action, such as imposing a penalty.

terms.label: original jurisdiction
terms.gloss: A court's power to hear a case first, rather than review another court's decision on appeal. The Supreme Court has it for a few cases, such as disputes between states.

terms.label: other-acts (propensity) evidence
terms.gloss: Evidence of a person's other wrongs or acts. Evidence rules like Rule 404(b) bar using it just to show bad character, but allow it for other purposes, such as plan, motive, or identity.

terms.label: ouster
terms.gloss: Wrongfully shutting someone out of property they have a right to share or possess. In forum-clause cases, the old objection that a private agreement cannot strip ('oust') a court of its power.

terms.label: output contract
terms.gloss: A contract in which the buyer agrees to buy all of a product the seller produces, so the quantity is set by the seller's actual good-faith output.

terms.label: overbreadth
terms.gloss: A free-speech doctrine letting a court strike down a law that, besides any valid uses, forbids a substantial amount of protected speech.

terms.label: parens patriae
terms.gloss: Latin for 'parent of the country': a state's power to sue to protect its residents' general welfare, not just its own property or interests.

terms.label: parol evidence
terms.gloss: Evidence of terms agreed before or while a written contract was signed. The parol evidence rule bars using it to contradict, or sometimes add to, a writing meant as the final agreement.

terms.label: particularity (pleading fraud)
terms.gloss: The stricter pleading standard for fraud and mistake: the complaint must state specific facts, such as who said what, when, where, and how, not just general accusations.

terms.label: partition (of property)
terms.gloss: A court-ordered division of jointly owned property among its co-owners, or its sale with the money split, when they cannot agree.

terms.label: payment bond / performance bond
terms.gloss: A guarantee by a surety, usually a bonding or insurance company: a payment bond ensures a contractor's workers and suppliers get paid; a performance bond ensures the work gets done if the contractor fails.

terms.label: penalty clause
terms.gloss: A payment a contract demands for breach that is far out of line with the likely or actual harm. U.S. courts refuse to enforce it.

terms.label: per curiam
terms.gloss: Latin for 'by the court': an opinion issued in the name of the whole court, with no individual judge named as author.

terms.label: per se
terms.gloss: Latin for 'by itself': automatically, without further proof. A per se rule treats certain conduct as unlawful in every case, whatever the circumstances.

terms.label: peremptory challenge (strike)
terms.gloss: A party's limited right to remove a potential juror without giving a reason, though never because of the juror's race or sex.

terms.label: permissive counterclaim
terms.gloss: A defendant's claim against the plaintiff that does not arise from the same events as the plaintiff's claim, so it may be raised now or saved for a separate suit.

terms.label: personal jurisdiction
terms.gloss: A court's power over a particular defendant, usually based on the defendant's connections with the state where the court sits, so its judgment can bind that defendant.

terms.label: personal representative
terms.gloss: The person appointed to manage a dead person's estate, such as an executor named in a will or an administrator chosen by a court.

terms.label: plain error
terms.gloss: An obvious mistake serious enough that an appeals court may correct it even though no one objected at trial.

terms.label: plat
terms.gloss: A recorded map dividing a tract of land into numbered lots, streets, and other parcels.

terms.label: plausibility standard (pleading)
terms.gloss: The federal pleading standard from Twombly (2007) and Iqbal (2009): a complaint must allege enough facts to make liability reasonable to infer, not merely conceivable.

terms.label: plea in abatement
terms.gloss: An older pleading objecting to where, when, or how a suit was brought, such as defective service, without denying the claim itself. Success ends or pauses that suit but allows refiling.

terms.label: pleading
terms.gloss: A formal written statement filed in a lawsuit setting out a party's claims or defenses, chiefly the complaint and the answer.

terms.label: plenary
terms.gloss: Full and complete, without limits. A plenary trial or review is a full one, and plenary authority is power over the whole subject.

terms.label: plurality opinion
terms.gloss: The lead opinion when no single opinion wins a majority of the judges. It announces the result, but its reasoning usually binds later courts less firmly.

terms.label: pocket veto
terms.gloss: A President's defeat of a bill by not signing it within ten days when Congress's adjournment prevents its return. Unlike a regular veto, Congress cannot override it.

terms.label: police power
terms.gloss: A state's broad authority to make laws protecting public health, safety, morals, and welfare. Despite the name, it is not limited to police or law enforcement.

terms.label: political question doctrine
terms.gloss: The rule that courts will not decide certain issues because the Constitution leaves them to Congress or the President, or because no workable legal standard exists.

terms.label: possessory lien
terms.gloss: A right to keep someone's goods until paid for work done on them, as a repair shop may hold a car until the bill is paid.

terms.label: postea
terms.gloss: In old English practice, the note on the trial record reporting the jury's verdict. Directing the postea to a party meant judgment would be entered for that party.

terms.label: power of appointment
terms.gloss: Authority, given by a will or trust, to choose who will receive certain property. The holder exercises it by naming recipients, often in the holder's own will.

terms.label: praemunire
terms.gloss: A medieval English statute and offense punishing anyone who used an outside authority, usually the Pope's courts, to undercut the King's courts. Penalties included forfeiture of property and loss of royal protection.

terms.label: prayer for relief
terms.gloss: The part of a complaint or petition stating what the plaintiff asks the court to order, such as money damages or an injunction. Not a religious request.

terms.label: pre-existing duty rule
terms.gloss: The rule that promising or doing only what one is already legally bound to do is not consideration, so it cannot support the other side's new promise.

terms.label: preclusion
terms.gloss: The rule that a final judgment bars relitigating claims or issues already decided, in later suits between the same parties or those closely tied to them. It covers claim and issue preclusion.

terms.label: predicate offense
terms.gloss: An earlier crime or conviction that a statute requires before it applies, such as a prior felony conviction that triggers a ban on owning guns.

terms.label: predominance (Rule 23(b)(3))
terms.gloss: For a class action seeking money, the requirement that questions common to the class outweigh questions that would have to be answered separately for each member.

terms.label: preemption
terms.gloss: The principle that valid federal law overrides state law, including state-law claims, when Congress says so expressly, when the two conflict, or when Congress has occupied the whole field.

terms.label: prejudice (harm to a party)
terms.gloss: Harm to a party's legal position, such as unfair surprise, lost evidence, or a weakened case. A dismissal 'with prejudice' is final: the claim cannot be brought again.

terms.label: preliminary injunction
terms.gloss: A temporary court order issued early in a case to prevent serious harm while the lawsuit is decided. The requester usually must show a likely win and harm money could not repair.

terms.label: preponderance of the evidence
terms.gloss: The usual standard of proof in civil cases: the side with the burden must show its version is more likely true than not.

terms.label: prerogative writ
terms.gloss: An extraordinary order, such as mandamus (commanding an official to perform a duty), issued at a high court's discretion to control officials or lower courts, not as of right.

terms.label: presentment (to the President)
terms.gloss: Sending a bill passed by both houses of Congress to the President to sign or veto. The Constitution requires this step before any bill becomes law.

terms.label: prima facie
terms.gloss: Latin for 'at first sight': enough evidence to prove a point, or to win, unless the other side rebuts it.

terms.label: prima facie tort
terms.gloss: A tort recognized in some states, notably New York, for intentionally harming someone without justification through otherwise lawful acts that cause specific money loss.

terms.label: principal (agency)
terms.gloss: In agency law, the person or business on whose behalf an agent acts and who can be bound by what the agent does within its authority.

terms.label: prior art
terms.gloss: In patent law, everything already publicly known before an invention, such as earlier patents and publications, used to judge whether it is new and not obvious.

terms.label: prior restraint
terms.gloss: Government action that stops speech before it happens, such as a licensing requirement or a court order barring publication, rather than punishing it afterward. Courts presume such restraints unconstitutional.

terms.label: private right of action
terms.gloss: The right of a private person, rather than the government, to sue to enforce a statute. When the statute is silent, courts decide whether Congress meant to allow one.

terms.label: privilege (evidence)
terms.gloss: A legal right to keep certain information, such as confidential lawyer or official communications, out of evidence and discovery even when it is relevant.

terms.label: privity
terms.gloss: A close, legally recognized relationship between parties, such as being the two sides of one contract, or sharing interests so closely that one is bound by a judgment against the other.

terms.label: pro hac vice
terms.gloss: Permission for a lawyer not licensed in a court's jurisdiction to appear in one particular case there. Latin for 'for this occasion'.

terms.label: probable cause
terms.gloss: A reasonable, fact-based ground for believing something, such as that a crime occurred or that a claim is likely to succeed. It requires more than suspicion but much less than proof.

terms.label: probative
terms.gloss: Tending to prove something. Evidence has probative value when it makes a disputed fact more or less likely.

terms.label: procedendo
terms.gloss: A higher court's order sending a case back to a lower court to go forward. In some states it issues when an appeal ends, much like a mandate.

terms.label: promissory estoppel
terms.gloss: Enforcing a promise that lacks a bargained-for exchange because the promisor should have expected reliance, the person promised did reasonably rely on it, and only enforcement can avoid injustice.

terms.label: promissory fraud
terms.gloss: Fraud committed by making a promise one does not intend to keep at the time it is made, so that the listener relies on it.

terms.label: property interest (due process)
terms.gloss: A legal entitlement, such as a job that can be ended only for cause or ongoing government benefits, that due process protects, so government must use fair procedures before ending it.

terms.label: prospectus
terms.gloss: In securities law, a document offering stock or other securities for sale to the public and describing the company and the investment. Federal law requires one for most public offerings.

terms.label: proximate cause
terms.gloss: A cause closely enough connected to the harm that the law holds the actor responsible, usually because that kind of harm was a foreseeable result of the conduct.

terms.label: prudential standing
terms.gloss: Court-made limits on who may sue, beyond the Constitution's minimum. The Supreme Court has since recast some, like the zone-of-interests test, as questions of what the statute allows.

terms.label: public domain (land)
terms.gloss: Land owned by the federal government and not yet granted to private owners. Not the copyright sense of material anyone may use.

terms.label: public figure (defamation)
terms.gloss: In defamation law, a famous person, or one who stepped into a public controversy. To win, they must prove the speaker knew the statement was false or recklessly disregarded the truth.

terms.label: public forum (forum analysis)
terms.gloss: Free-speech categories for government property. In traditional public forums like streets and parks, content-based limits face strict scrutiny; in nonpublic forums, limits need only be reasonable and viewpoint-neutral.

terms.label: public rights doctrine
terms.gloss: The doctrine letting Congress assign certain disputes, typically between the government and individuals under federal law, to agencies or special courts without a jury or life-tenured judge.

terms.label: public use (takings)
terms.gloss: The constitutional limit that government may take private property only for a public use, read broadly as a public purpose such as a road or park, and must pay just compensation.

terms.label: publication (defamation)
terms.gloss: In defamation law, communicating a statement to at least one person other than its subject; no printing is needed. (Notice 'by publication' instead means notice printed in a newspaper.)

terms.label: punitive damages
terms.gloss: Money awarded beyond the plaintiff's actual loss to punish especially bad conduct and discourage it. Usually unavailable for an ordinary breach of contract.

terms.label: purposeful availment
terms.gloss: A defendant's deliberate choice to do business in, or aim conduct at, a state, which can make it fair for that state's courts to hear related claims against it.

terms.label: qualified immunity
terms.gloss: A defense shielding government officials from personal liability for damages unless they violated a clearly established right that a reasonable official would have known about.

terms.label: quantum meruit
terms.gloss: Latin for 'as much as deserved': recovery of the reasonable value of work or services provided, even without an enforceable contract to pay for them.

terms.label: quasi-contract
terms.gloss: An obligation the law imposes, without any real agreement, to pay for a benefit received so the recipient is not unjustly enriched.

terms.label: quasi in rem
terms.gloss: Jurisdiction based on a defendant's property in the state, used to decide a claim against that defendant, with any recovery limited to that property.

terms.label: quasi-judicial
terms.gloss: Court-like: describes an agency or official that holds hearings, finds facts, and decides individual disputes, though it is not a court.

terms.label: quasi-legislative
terms.gloss: Describes an agency's power to make general rules that work like statutes, even though the agency is not a legislature.

terms.label: qui tam
terms.gloss: A lawsuit a private person brings on the government's behalf, usually against someone defrauding it, in exchange for a share of any recovery.

terms.label: quiet title action
terms.gloss: A lawsuit asking a court to declare who owns land and to end competing claims to it.

terms.label: quitclaim deed
terms.gloss: A deed transferring whatever interest the seller has in the land, if any, with no promise that the title is good.

terms.label: quo warranto
terms.gloss: Latin for 'by what authority': a court proceeding challenging a person's right to hold a public office, or a corporation's right to exercise its powers.

terms.label: racial steering
terms.gloss: In fair-housing law, guiding home seekers toward or away from neighborhoods or buildings because of their race. The Fair Housing Act forbids it.

terms.label: rational-basis review
terms.gloss: The most lenient test of whether a law is constitutional: it is upheld if rationally related to any legitimate government purpose. Most laws pass it.

terms.label: real party in interest
terms.gloss: The person who actually holds the legal right being enforced, and so generally must be the one who brings the suit (federal Rule 17).

terms.label: real property
terms.gloss: Land and anything permanently attached to it, such as buildings, as opposed to movable personal property. 'Real' here does not mean genuine.

terms.label: reasonable expectations doctrine
terms.gloss: An insurance rule, used in some states, that enforces the coverage an ordinary policyholder would reasonably expect, even against the policy's fine print.

terms.label: rebuttable presumption
terms.gloss: An assumption the law requires the judge or jury to make unless the opposing side offers enough evidence to overcome it.

terms.label: receiver (court-appointed)
terms.gloss: A neutral person a court appoints to take charge of and manage property, often a failing company's assets, during a lawsuit or insolvency, under the court's supervision.

terms.label: recital
terms.gloss: A statement in a contract, deed, or bond setting out background facts, such as the reasons for the deal or that payment was made. It usually is not itself a promise.

terms.label: recognition of judgments
terms.gloss: One court's acceptance of a judgment from another state or country as binding, so the matters it decided are not relitigated and it can be enforced there.

terms.label: record (of a case)
terms.gloss: Everything officially before a court in a case: the filed papers, the evidence admitted, and the transcripts. Decisions are made on what this file shows.

terms.label: recoupment
terms.gloss: A defendant's claim to reduce what it owes the plaintiff by the defendant's own damages arising from the same transaction.

terms.label: redressability
terms.gloss: The third standing requirement: it must be likely, not merely speculative, that a court ruling for the plaintiff would fix or lessen the claimed injury.

terms.label: referee (court-appointed)
terms.gloss: A person a court appoints to hear evidence, find facts, and report on or decide part of a case for the judge. Parties may also choose one to settle a technical dispute.

terms.label: reformation (of a writing)
terms.gloss: A court remedy that rewrites a contract or other document to match what the parties actually agreed, usually to fix a shared mistake or fraud.

terms.label: relation back
terms.gloss: The rule that an amended pleading can count as filed on the original's date if it arises from the same events, so a deadline that passed in between does not bar it.

terms.label: relator
terms.gloss: A private person who sues on the government's behalf and in its name, as in False Claims Act cases, and may share in any money recovered.

terms.label: reliance damages
terms.gloss: Money repaying what the injured party spent or gave up in reasonably relying on a broken promise, to restore it to where it stood before the promise.

terms.label: relief (court remedy)
terms.gloss: What a party asks a court to order, such as money damages, an injunction, or a declaration of rights. Not comfort or easing.
except: complete relief from many forms of pain

terms.label: remand
terms.gloss: To send a case back for further action: from an appeals court to a lower court or agency, or from federal court to the state court it was removed from.

terms.label: remittitur
terms.gloss: A judge's order reducing a jury's damages award the judge finds excessive, usually giving the plaintiff a choice between the lower amount and a new trial.

terms.label: removal (of a case)
terms.gloss: A defendant's transfer of a lawsuit filed in state court to the federal trial court for that area, allowed when the case could have been filed in federal court originally.

terms.label: removal power
terms.gloss: The President's authority to fire executive officials. Congress sometimes limits it, letting certain officers be fired only 'for cause', such as neglect of duty or misconduct.

terms.label: rendering state
terms.gloss: The state whose court issued a judgment now being relied on elsewhere. Its rules usually decide how binding that judgment is in other courts.

terms.label: replevin
terms.gloss: A lawsuit to get back specific personal property that someone is wrongfully holding, rather than money for its value.

terms.label: repose
terms.gloss: Freedom from being sued or pressed on a claim, as when time limits bar old lawsuits, final judgments end disputes, or a creditor agrees to wait before collecting.

terms.label: repudiation (of a contract)
terms.gloss: A party's clear statement or act showing it will not perform its contract. If it comes before performance is due ('anticipatory'), the other side may treat it as a breach immediately.

terms.label: repugnant (to a law)
terms.gloss: So directly in conflict with another law that both cannot stand, as when a state statute contradicts valid federal law and must give way. Here it does not mean disgusting.

terms.label: requirements contract
terms.gloss: A contract in which a buyer agrees to buy all it needs of a product from one seller, so the quantity depends on the buyer's actual good-faith needs.

terms.label: res gestae
terms.gloss: Latin for 'things done.' An older evidence label for statements made as part of, or right alongside, the event in question, which courts sometimes admitted despite hearsay rules.

terms.label: res judicata
terms.gloss: Latin for 'a matter judged': once a final judgment decides a claim, the same parties cannot sue again on it, even on parts they could have raised before, and often cannot reargue issues decided.

terms.label: rescission
terms.gloss: Undoing a contract as if it never existed, with each side returning what it received. Usually available for fraud, mistake, duress, or a serious breach.

terms.label: residuary estate (residue)
terms.gloss: What remains of a dead person's estate after debts, expenses, taxes, and specific gifts are paid. A will's residuary clause names who receives it.

terms.label: respondent
terms.gloss: The party who must answer a petition or appeal, which on appeal can be either original side. In a writ proceeding it may be the judge or official being challenged.

terms.label: Restatement
terms.gloss: A respected summary of the common law in a field, written by the American Law Institute. Courts often follow it, but it is not binding.

terms.label: restitution
terms.gloss: A remedy requiring a party to give back a benefit it received, or its value, measured by what that party gained rather than what the other side lost.

terms.label: restraint of trade
terms.gloss: An agreement or practice that limits competition, such as rivals fixing prices or dividing markets. Section 1 of the Sherman Act forbids unreasonable restraints.

terms.label: restrictive covenant
terms.gloss: A promise limiting what someone may do, such as an employee's promise not to compete after leaving or a landowner's promise about how land may be used.

terms.label: reviewability
terms.gloss: Whether a court can examine and correct a decision. Some agency choices are presumed beyond review; an order is 'effectively unreviewable' when waiting to appeal would make review useless.

terms.label: ripeness
terms.gloss: Whether a dispute has developed enough for a court to decide it now, rather than depending on future events that may never happen.

terms.label: rough proportionality
terms.gloss: The test, from Dolan v. City of Tigard (1994), that the government must show a permit condition is roughly related, in kind and size, to the project's actual impact.

terms.label: Federal Rule 11
terms.gloss: The federal rule that signing a court filing certifies, after reasonable inquiry, that it has factual and legal support and a proper purpose. Courts may penalize violations.

terms.label: Federal Rule 12(b)(6)
terms.gloss: The federal rule letting a party ask the court to dismiss a claim that, even if every fact alleged is true, states no legal basis for relief.

terms.label: Federal Rule 23 (class actions)
terms.gloss: The federal class-action rule. It sets when one or a few people may sue for a large group, and how courts certify, notify, supervise, and settle such suits.

terms.label: Federal Rule 23(b)(3)
terms.gloss: The main federal class action for money damages, allowed only if common questions predominate over individual ones and a class suit is the superior method. Members may opt out.

terms.label: Federal Rule 23(f)
terms.gloss: The federal rule letting a court of appeals choose to hear an immediate appeal from an order granting or denying class certification, before the case ends.

terms.label: Federal Rule 50
terms.gloss: The federal rule letting a judge decide a jury case against a party, before or after the verdict, when no reasonable jury could find for that party on the evidence.

terms.label: Federal Rule 52(a)
terms.gloss: The federal rule requiring a judge who decides facts without a jury to state findings and conclusions. Appeals courts may set aside those findings only if clearly mistaken.

terms.label: Federal Rule 54(b)
terms.gloss: The federal rule letting a court enter final, immediately appealable judgment on some claims or parties before the whole case ends, if there is no just reason for delay.

terms.label: Federal Rule 56 (summary judgment)
terms.gloss: The federal rule for deciding a claim without trial when there is no genuine dispute about any important fact and one side is entitled to win under the law.

terms.label: Federal Rule 59
terms.gloss: The federal rule for asking the trial court, within 28 days after judgment, to order a new trial or to alter or amend its judgment.

terms.label: Rule 60(b)
terms.gloss: The federal rule letting a court reopen a final judgment for listed reasons, such as mistake, newly found evidence, fraud, or a void judgment, within time limits.

terms.label: Federal Rule 8 (general pleading)
terms.gloss: The federal rule setting the basic pleading standard: a complaint needs only a short and plain statement of the claim showing the pleader is entitled to relief.

terms.label: Federal Rule 9(b)
terms.gloss: The federal rule requiring a party alleging fraud or mistake to state the circumstances with particularity, such as who said what, when, and how, not just general charges.

terms.label: rule against perpetuities
terms.gloss: An old property rule voiding a future interest unless it is certain to vest (become fixed), if at all, within a life in being when it was created plus 21 years.

terms.label: rule nisi / rule absolute
terms.gloss: An older form of court order that becomes final unless the other side shows good reason against it. When no such reason is shown, the court 'makes the rule absolute.'

terms.label: rule of lenity
terms.gloss: The principle that when a criminal law is truly ambiguous, courts adopt the reading more favorable to the defendant.

terms.label: rulemaking
terms.gloss: An agency's process of making general rules that apply going forward, as opposed to deciding one case. Usually the agency publishes a proposal and takes public comment first.

terms.label: safe harbor
terms.gloss: A provision shielding a party from liability or a penalty if stated conditions are met, such as Rule 11's 21 days to withdraw a challenged filing before a sanctions motion may be filed.

terms.label: satisfaction (of a debt or claim)
terms.gloss: Payment or performance accepted as fully discharging a debt or claim, so that nothing more can be demanded on it.

terms.label: saving clause
terms.gloss: A provision in a statute or rule preserving certain existing rights, remedies, or defenses that the rest of it might otherwise displace, such as ordinary contract defenses under the Federal Arbitration Act.

terms.label: scienter
terms.gloss: A guilty state of mind: knowing that something is wrong or false, or acting with reckless disregard for the truth. Fraud claims, including securities fraud, require it.

terms.label: scintilla
terms.gloss: A tiny trace. Evidence amounting to only a 'scintilla' is not enough to support a jury verdict, defeat summary judgment, or sustain an agency's finding.

terms.label: seal (contract under seal)
terms.gloss: A formal mark on a signed document. Traditionally a promise under seal was binding even without consideration, something given in exchange; many states have abolished or limited that rule.

terms.label: seasonable
terms.gloss: Timely: done within the time agreed or, if none, within a reasonable time. A Uniform Commercial Code term; nothing to do with seasons.

terms.label: security interest
terms.gloss: A creditor's legal right in specific property of the debtor that backs a debt, letting the creditor take or sell that property if the debt is not paid.

terms.label: sequestration (of property)
terms.gloss: A court-ordered seizure of a defendant's property, held while the case proceeds; often used against a nonresident's local property to pressure them to come and defend.

terms.label: service of process
terms.gloss: Formally delivering court papers, usually the summons and complaint, to a party. It gives notice of the suit and is generally required before the court can act against that party.

terms.label: set aside
terms.gloss: To cancel or nullify a verdict, judgment, order, or agency rule, so it no longer has legal effect. Not 'save for later'.

terms.label: setoff
terms.gloss: Reducing what one party owes another by a separate debt the other party owes back to it, so only the difference is paid.

terms.label: settlor
terms.gloss: The person who creates a trust by handing property to a trustee to manage for the beneficiaries.

terms.label: severability
terms.gloss: Whether the valid parts of a contract or statute can stand when one part is held invalid. A severability clause states that the rest should survive.

terms.label: sitting by designation
terms.gloss: A judge from another court who is temporarily assigned to help decide a case, such as a district judge joining an appeals panel.

terms.label: situs
terms.gloss: The place where property, including intangible property like stock, is treated as located for legal purposes, such as deciding which state may tax it or exercise power over it.

terms.label: Skidmore deference
terms.gloss: Giving an agency's interpretation weight only as far as its reasoning, thoroughness, and consistency persuade the court. It is respect, not binding deference.

terms.label: slayer rule
terms.gloss: The principle that a person who intentionally and wrongfully kills another cannot inherit from, or otherwise profit from, the victim's death.

terms.label: sounds in
terms.gloss: Is in its legal nature: a claim that 'sounds in fraud' is really a fraud claim, whatever it is called, and follows fraud's rules.

terms.label: sovereign acts doctrine
terms.gloss: A defense shielding the federal government from contract liability when its public and general act, not one aimed at its own contracts, prevents performance.

terms.label: sovereign immunity
terms.gloss: A government's protection from being sued without its own consent. The United States and the states each have it, though it can be waived.

terms.label: special appearance
terms.gloss: Coming to court only to challenge the court's power over the defendant, such as defective service or lack of personal jurisdiction, without submitting to that power.

terms.label: special damages
terms.gloss: Damages for particular losses that do not follow automatically from the wrong, such as lost earnings or specific expenses; they usually must be specifically pleaded and proved.

terms.label: special master
terms.gloss: A person, often a lawyer or retired judge, appointed by a court to handle part of a case, such as gathering evidence, overseeing a settlement, or recommending findings.

terms.label: special verdict
terms.gloss: A jury verdict answering specific written questions of fact, leaving the judge to apply the law, rather than simply naming the winner.

terms.label: specific jurisdiction
terms.gloss: A court's power over an out-of-state defendant for a claim that arises from or relates to the defendant's own deliberate contacts with the state.

terms.label: specific performance
terms.gloss: A court order requiring a party to actually do what the contract promised, such as transfer land, instead of paying damages.

terms.label: spontaneous exclamation
terms.gloss: A statement blurted out under the stress of a startling event (an excited utterance). Courts may admit it despite the hearsay rule against out-of-court statements, since there was no time to invent it.

terms.label: stakeholder (interpleader)
terms.gloss: In interpleader, the party holding money or property that several others claim. It asks the court to decide among the claimants so it does not have to pay twice.

terms.label: standard of review
terms.gloss: How much deference an appeals court gives a lower court's or agency's decision, ranging from a fresh look (de novo) to reversal only for clear error or abuse of discretion.

terms.label: standing
terms.gloss: A party's right to bring a particular lawsuit. In federal court it usually requires a concrete injury, caused by the defendant, that a court ruling could fix.

terms.label: standing offer
terms.gloss: An offer that stays open for repeated acceptances, so each order placed under it can form a separate contract until the offer is withdrawn.

terms.label: stare decisis
terms.gloss: Latin for 'to stand by things decided': courts should follow earlier decisions on the same legal question unless there is strong reason to depart.

terms.label: state action
terms.gloss: Conduct that counts as the government's, which most constitutional rights require; purely private conduct usually does not qualify.

terms.label: case stated (special case)
terms.gloss: A written statement of agreed or found facts sent to a higher court so it can decide only the legal question, used in old English practice and in arbitration appeals.

terms.label: statement of basis and purpose
terms.gloss: The explanation an agency must publish with a new rule under APA § 553(c), setting out its major policy choices and the reasons for them.

terms.label: statute of frauds
terms.gloss: A rule requiring certain contracts, such as land sales and deals that cannot be completed within a year, to be backed by a signed writing to be enforceable.

terms.label: statutory damages
terms.gloss: Damages in an amount, or within a range, set by a statute for each violation, which a court may award without proof of the actual amount of harm.

terms.label: stay (court order)
terms.gloss: A court order pausing a lawsuit, the enforcement of a judgment, or an official action for a time, often until an appeal or another proceeding ends.

terms.label: stipulation
terms.gloss: A formal agreement between the parties to a case that a fact or issue is settled, so it need not be proved. In a contract, 'stipulated' means specified.

terms.label: stream of commerce
terms.gloss: A theory that a manufacturer whose products flow through distributors into a state, expecting sales there, may be sued there. Justices disagree on whether more deliberate targeting is required.

terms.label: strict liability
terms.gloss: Legal responsibility for harm without any need to prove fault, carelessness, or intent, as for certain dangerous activities or defective products.

terms.label: strict scrutiny
terms.gloss: The toughest test courts use for laws burdening fundamental rights or classifying by race: the government must show the law is narrowly tailored to serve a compelling interest.

terms.label: sua sponte
terms.gloss: Latin for 'of its own accord': action a court takes on its own initiative, without any party asking for it.

terms.label: subject-matter jurisdiction
terms.gloss: A court's power to hear a particular kind of case. Federal courts have it only for categories the Constitution and Congress allow; parties cannot create it by consent.

terms.label: subpoena
terms.gloss: A court order requiring a person to testify or to produce documents or other evidence, with a penalty for refusing.

terms.label: subrogation
terms.gloss: Taking over another person's legal rights. For example, an insurer that pays a loss steps into the insured's shoes and can sue whoever caused it.

terms.label: substantial evidence
terms.gloss: A deferential standard for reviewing agency or jury findings: enough relevant evidence that a reasonable person could accept it as adequate support for the conclusion.

terms.label: substantial impairment (UCC)
terms.gloss: Under the UCC, a defect or breach serious enough to significantly reduce the value of an installment or of the whole contract to the buyer, allowing rejection, revocation of acceptance, or cancellation.

terms.label: substantial performance
terms.gloss: Performance that meets a contract's essential purpose despite minor flaws. It lets the performing party recover the price, minus damages for the shortfall.

terms.label: substantive canon
terms.gloss: A rule for reading statutes that favors a particular value or result, such as avoiding constitutional doubts or reading criminal laws narrowly, rather than reflecting how ordinary language works.

terms.label: substantive due process
terms.gloss: The doctrine that the Due Process Clauses protect certain fundamental rights from government interference however fair the procedures, not just the right to a fair process.

terms.label: substantive law
terms.gloss: The law that defines people's rights and duties, such as the rules of contracts or injury claims, as opposed to procedural law, which governs how cases are run.

terms.label: summary judgment
terms.gloss: A ruling that decides a case, or part of it, without a trial because there is no genuine dispute over any important fact and one side is entitled to win under the law.

terms.label: superiority (Rule 23(b)(3))
terms.gloss: For a class action seeking money, the requirement that one group lawsuit be better than separate suits or other methods for fairly and efficiently resolving the dispute.

terms.label: supplemental jurisdiction
terms.gloss: A federal court's power to hear extra claims, usually under state law, that it could not hear alone, because they arise from the same facts as a claim properly before it.

terms.label: surcharge (a trustee)
terms.gloss: To order a trustee or other fiduciary to repay losses its mismanagement caused.

terms.label: surety
terms.gloss: A person or company that promises to pay a debt or perform a duty if the main party fails to, such as a bond company backing a contractor.

terms.label: surplusage
terms.gloss: Wording that adds nothing and has no legal effect. Courts generally avoid reading a statute so that any of its words would be pointless, though this is a presumption, not an absolute rule.

terms.label: suspect classification
terms.gloss: A government line drawn by race, national origin, or a similar trait. Courts presume it is improper and uphold it only if narrowly tailored to serve a compelling government goal.

terms.label: Take Care Clause
terms.gloss: The constitutional command that the President "take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed," cited in disputes over presidential control of law enforcement and executive officials.

terms.label: take-nothing judgment
terms.gloss: A final judgment that the plaintiff recovers nothing from the defendant.

terms.label: taking (of property)
terms.gloss: Government seizure of private property, or regulation so severe it has the same effect. The Fifth Amendment requires the government to pay just compensation for it.

terms.label: basis (tax)
terms.gloss: For tax purposes, an owner's investment in property, usually its cost, adjusted over time. The taxable gain on a sale is the amount received minus the basis.

terms.label: tax deficiency
terms.gloss: Tax the government determines is owed beyond the amount shown on the taxpayer's return. The taxpayer can usually contest it in the Tax Court before paying.

terms.label: taxed costs
terms.gloss: Not a government tax: routine court expenses, such as filing and witness fees but usually not lawyers' fees, that the losing side is ordered to repay the winner. 'Taxing' costs means fixing that amount.

terms.label: temporary restraining order
terms.gloss: A short-term emergency order, sometimes issued without hearing from the other side, that keeps things as they are until the court can hold a hearing on a longer-lasting order.

terms.label: tenancy in common
terms.gloss: Shared ownership in which each co-owner holds a separate share. At death, a share passes to the owner's heirs or will beneficiaries, not to the surviving co-owners.

terms.label: tender (of performance)
terms.gloss: An unconditional offer to perform or pay what is owed, made with present ability to do so. Under the UCC 'perfect tender' rule, a buyer may reject goods that fail in any way to match the contract.

terms.label: tender offer
terms.gloss: A public offer to buy a company's shares directly from its shareholders, usually above market price and for a limited time.

terms.label: term of art
terms.gloss: A word or phrase with a settled specialized meaning in law or a trade, which is read in that sense rather than its everyday one.

terms.label: testamentary
terms.gloss: Relating to a will. A testamentary gift takes effect at death and usually must meet the formal requirements for wills; testamentary capacity is the mental ability needed to make one.

terms.label: testator
terms.gloss: A person who has made a will, usually one who has since died. Testatrix is an older term for a woman.

terms.label: third-party beneficiary
terms.gloss: Someone who is not a party to a contract but whom the contracting parties intended to benefit, and who may therefore be able to enforce it.

terms.label: third-party (nondebtor) release
terms.gloss: A bankruptcy-plan provision ending creditors' claims against people other than the bankrupt company, such as its owners. The Supreme Court held in 2024 that bankruptcy law does not allow nonconsensual ones.

terms.label: third-party standing
terms.gloss: Permission to assert someone else's legal rights, allowed when the litigant is itself injured, closely tied to that person, and that person faces obstacles to suing.

terms.label: tolling
terms.gloss: Pausing a legal deadline, usually a statute of limitations (the time limit for suing), so the clock stops running for a while.

terms.label: tort
terms.gloss: A civil wrong, other than breaking a contract, that injures someone, such as careless injury, trespass, or harming a reputation, and lets the victim sue for compensation.

terms.label: tortfeasor
terms.gloss: A person who commits a tort, a civil wrong such as careless injury, that the victim can sue over. Joint tortfeasors together cause a single harm.

terms.label: tortious interference
terms.gloss: The civil wrong of intentionally and improperly disrupting someone's contract or business relationship with a third party, causing loss.

terms.label: traceability
terms.gloss: The second standing requirement: the plaintiff's injury must be fairly traceable to, meaning caused by, the defendant's challenged conduct, not someone else's independent choices.

terms.label: transitory action
terms.gloss: A lawsuit, such as one for personal injury or a debt, that may be brought wherever the defendant can be found, unlike a local action tied to land in one place.

terms.label: treble damages
terms.gloss: Damages tripled by statute: the court multiplies the actual loss by three to punish and deter, as under antitrust law and some consumer-protection laws.

terms.label: trial de novo
terms.gloss: A completely new trial that decides the facts and law afresh, as if no earlier hearing had taken place.

terms.label: trover
terms.gloss: An old form of lawsuit to recover the value of personal property someone wrongfully took or kept, rather than the item itself. It is the ancestor of today's conversion claim.

terms.label: trust land (Indian)
terms.gloss: Land the United States holds legal title to for the benefit of a tribe or individual Indians, which limits its sale and shields it from most state taxes.

terms.label: accounting (by a trustee)
terms.gloss: A trustee's formal report to a court of how it handled trust property. Once the court approves it, beneficiaries usually cannot later sue over what it disclosed.

terms.label: typicality (Rule 23(a)(3))
terms.gloss: The class-action requirement that the representatives' claims be typical of the class, arising from the same conduct and resting on the same legal theory as other members' claims.

terms.label: ultimate fact
terms.gloss: A fact that directly decides an element of a claim or defense, such as whether an employer discriminated. It is usually inferred from more basic, evidentiary facts.

terms.label: ultra vires
terms.gloss: Latin for 'beyond the powers': an act by an agency, official, or corporation that exceeds the legal authority it was given.

terms.label: unclean hands
terms.gloss: A defense to equitable remedies, such as injunctions: a court may refuse help to a party that acted unfairly or in bad faith in the very matter it sues about.

terms.label: unconscionability
terms.gloss: A court's refusal to enforce a contract or term that is shockingly one-sided, usually because of both an unfair bargaining process and harsh terms.

terms.label: undivided interest
terms.gloss: A co-owner's share in the whole of a property, rather than in any particular part of it.

terms.label: undue influence
terms.gloss: Unfair persuasion by someone in a position of trust or dominance that overcomes another's free choice, leaving the resulting contract or gift open to being undone.

terms.label: unilateral contract
terms.gloss: A contract in which the offer can be accepted only by doing the requested act, not by promising to do it, such as a reward for returning a lost dog.

terms.label: unilateral mistake
terms.gloss: An error about a basic fact of a deal made by only one side. It rarely undoes a contract unless the other side knew of or caused it, or enforcement would be grossly unfair.

terms.label: universal injunction
terms.gloss: A court order blocking enforcement of a law or policy against everyone, not just those who sued. In 2025 the Supreme Court held such orders likely exceed federal courts' equitable power.

terms.label: unjust enrichment
terms.gloss: A claim that one person received a benefit at another's expense in circumstances that make it unfair to keep without paying. The usual remedy is restitution: returning the benefit's value.

terms.label: unlawful detainer
terms.gloss: A fast-track court proceeding to evict someone, usually a tenant, who stays in possession of property without the right to.

terms.label: unmistakability doctrine
terms.gloss: The rule that a government contract will not be read as surrendering the government's power to change the law unless it does so in unmistakable terms.

terms.label: unpublished opinion
terms.gloss: A court decision not designated for publication in the official reports. It usually binds only the parties and does not serve as precedent.

terms.label: unseaworthiness
terms.gloss: A ship owner's duty, owed even without any carelessness, to provide a vessel, gear, and crew reasonably fit for their use. Injured seamen, and until 1972 longshoremen, could sue for its breach.

terms.label: usage of trade
terms.gloss: A practice so regularly followed in a trade or place that parties are expected to have meant it, so it can explain or add to a written contract.

terms.label: vacate (vacatur)
terms.gloss: To cancel or set aside a court's judgment or order so it no longer has effect, often sending the matter back for a fresh decision. Vacatur is the noun.

terms.label: vacation (of a street or plat)
terms.gloss: The official cancellation of a public street or recorded land dedication, ending the public's rights so the land returns to private use. Not a holiday.

terms.label: venire
terms.gloss: The group of people summoned for jury duty from which a trial jury is picked. An old writ, 'venire facias,' ordered such a group assembled.

terms.label: venire facias de novo
terms.gloss: Latin for 'cause to come anew': an old writ summoning a new jury, and so a new trial, because the first verdict was defective.

terms.label: venue
terms.gloss: The proper place for a case to be heard, such as a particular federal district or county. Statutes set it, separately from whether the court has power over the case.

terms.label: vicarious liability
terms.gloss: Legal responsibility for someone else's wrong because of a relationship, such as an employer's for an employee's on-the-job conduct, without personal fault.

terms.label: virtual (equitable) adoption
terms.gloss: A doctrine in some states treating a child as legally adopted, usually for inheritance, when an adult promised to adopt and acted as a parent but never formally did.

terms.label: virtual representation
terms.gloss: A theory that a nonparty is bound by an earlier judgment because someone with closely aligned interests already litigated. The Supreme Court rejected it for federal-court judgments in Taylor v. Sturgell (2008).

terms.label: void for vagueness
terms.gloss: The due-process rule that a law is invalid if it is too unclear to give fair notice of what it forbids, or if it invites arbitrary enforcement.

terms.label: voidable
terms.gloss: Valid unless and until one party chooses to cancel it. A contract made by a minor or induced by fraud, for example, binds until that party backs out.

terms.label: voir dire
terms.gloss: Questioning of potential jurors by the judge or lawyers before trial to uncover bias and choose the jury.

terms.label: voluntary cessation
terms.gloss: A defendant's stopping the challenged conduct after being sued. It usually does not end the case unless the defendant shows the conduct cannot reasonably be expected to recur.

terms.label: warranty deed
terms.gloss: A deed in which the seller guarantees good title to the land and promises to defend the buyer against others' claims to it.

terms.label: well-pleaded complaint rule
terms.gloss: The rule that a case arises under federal law, for federal-court jurisdiction, only if the plaintiff's own claim, not an expected defense, rests on federal law.

terms.label: with prejudice
terms.gloss: Final: a dismissal or ruling that bars the party from ever bringing the same claim again. 'Prejudice' here has nothing to do with bias.

terms.label: without prejudice
terms.gloss: Leaving the door open: a dismissal or denial that does not stop the party from refiling the claim or renewing the request later. 'Prejudice' here has nothing to do with bias.

terms.label: work product
terms.gloss: Materials prepared by or for a party in anticipation of litigation, such as a lawyer's notes and memos. The other side can get them only by showing substantial need and no other source.

terms.label: writ
terms.gloss: A formal written court order commanding a person, official, or lower court to do, or stop doing, a specific act.

terms.label: writ of error
terms.gloss: An older form of appeal in which a higher court reviewed only legal mistakes shown in the lower court's record, not the facts.

terms.label: writ of prohibition
terms.gloss: An order from a higher court directing a lower court not to act beyond its authority in a case.

terms.label: yellow-dog contract
terms.gloss: An employment agreement in which the worker promises not to join, or to leave, a labor union. The Norris-LaGuardia Act of 1932 made such promises unenforceable in federal courts.

terms.label: zone of interests
terms.gloss: A test asking whether a plaintiff's interest is among those the statute was meant to protect or regulate, so that the plaintiff may sue under it.
